The zero audit's exclusion list omits `108ab82d6` and `031c38bbc`; J1024 3.1 item 3 covers both.
108	
109	## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds
110	
111	**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.
112	
113	**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. No team text says the code generator, class loader or RTTI needs `Object` (archaeology §2.6, §5). The code reads the other way: Naden's dispatcher ignores a written `Any` bound as "meaningless" and checks any other (`OverloadSet.java:1516-1517`); `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` names an empty clause `Object` only in a generic method's name, which declaration and call compute alike. The team's texts after 2012-05-30 (Types, 05-31; Naden, 08-31; POPL 2019) do not carry `Object` as the default. So the setting is the compiled path's departure from the language's rule, L2, and ends by one line.
114	
115	**L2, the probe.** Under `Any`, generic functions, objects, traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase` at a pair or an arrow compile, load and run, making the same classes and the same bytecode as with `extends Any` written; the 23 `CompilerSystem` `.test` files pass under both settings; `ant testQuick` under `Any` gives 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side (one promotion, three pinned texts, four `where [\E extends Object\]` workarounds of row 412, one premise, one prelude limit). Under `Object`, `q = id((3, 4))` compiles and runs `id(3)`, printing `q + 1 = 4` (row 691 reached by row 412): the compile command as it stands can silently miscompile. `()` dies under either bound (row 339, confirmed by `javap`); a generic dotted method with a single tuple-typed parameter dies under either bound (new, `CodeGen.java:6250-6263`, the team's comment "when generics can be parametrized by tuples"). Neither depends on the bound.
116	
117	**L3.** `java.lang.Object` is translated to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`); natives are written against `fortress.AnyType.Any`; no team text ties Fortress `Object` to `java.lang.Object`. Java interoperability argues for `Any`, and the record never used an L3 ground for the bound. His hunch that layers were mixed is right in form; the crossing was L1→L2 on 09-20 (a WD sentence kept as the reason for a compiled-path setting), not L3→L1.
118	
119	**What he was told, and whether it changes the decision.** Told: that the compile path writes `Object` and this refuses tuples (true); that Steele switched the bound off in 2012 for the interpreter tests (true, half the story); that the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types (wrong: it puts arrows under `Object`); that "nothing in the code changes because of it" (wrong: `Shell.java:372`). Not told: that Steele turned it on for the compiled path as a setting on 05-30; the code that reads the bound; the sentence's absence from 1.0. Had he been told all of it, the question under P-26 would have been "is Steele's 2012 setting the team's later word on the language?", and the answer above is no. His yes rested on the tuples; the tuples decide it. The decision stands and is stronger.
120	
121	**Where the entry misstates.** "Functions" (rq 218): the WD puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does. "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure": the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting).
122	
123	**Defaults.** P-42 stands (his; no change). The flip lands in 22c as one small rung: `Shell.java:372` to `false`, `XXXImplicitBoundAny` promoted, three pinned diagnostics rewritten, four `comprises` tests written `where [\E\]`, `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`'s premise rewritten with row 653 named, `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` given `T extends Object` with a comment naming the prelude's `||` until the switch-over (the smallest edit that keeps the test's purpose; the other way is an `XXX` test). The probe's record actions: a ledger row for the tuple-domain dotted-method defect (section 12 of the ledger); row 339's "unverified" dropped; row 691's note; F-289 updated at the landing; the two FACTS the probe hands over. The flip is the coordinator's to schedule (P-42 promised it), named to him because he listed it among 22c's candidates.
124

126	
127	- **Why the framing is sound.** J1024 §6 called phase 3 done by P-33's letter with its exit restated, and named a wider checker zero for phase 4. His framing moves the library-text and checker items that make the zero honest into one closing batch, so that phase 3 exits with a zero the switch-over can use: over the thirteen, under the compile command's own setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way. That is the first of J1024's two phase-4 zeros, brought forward; the code generator's zero stays phase 4's. It is the right cut: everything in 22c is checker or library text; everything left is code generation, run time or natives.
128	- **The four rungs (defaults), with what each protects against:**
129	  1. **Row 816's repair (P-158):** the export check's count of every api member restored, 12 bodyless lines in five component traits. Without it 9 of 12 members die compiled with `NoSuchMethodError`. 1 rung.
130	  2. **Row 782:** the export check reads top-level symbolic operators (P-155 read to cover the export check, J1024 item 7's default yes), the double key fixed, the 9 headers matched (the component takes the api's types where the api cannot name the component's). Without it `#` and `:`, which build every range loop, die compiled. 1 rung.

132	  4. **The bound `Any` for `fortress compile`** (section 4). Without it phase 3's zero is a zero under a setting no command has (F-289), and the command can miscompile silently (row 691). 1 small rung; the 27 `CompilerSystem` tests need nothing (measured).
133	- **The exit gate for 22c:** the distance stage reports 0 over the thirteen with `#crash none`, run under the compile command's setting; the full gate green with the ten test edits.
134	- **Not in 22c, phase 4 before the names batch:** row 701 (the code generator's `where` clauses; four of five walls in the twelve are revival lines, and `fortress compile FortressLibrary` stops at the first), row 321 with the tuple-rendering device (needs his word), the 52 code-generator refusals (several rungs, sized by the planner), `System`'s 2 errors, and the natives (batch 23 first). The two phase-4 zeros stand as J1024 named them.

136	- **Default:** yes, 22c with the four rungs; phase 3 closes at its gate; the four open words to him stay open (P-58's informed yes; the 40 components' place; rq 35; rq 230). Consequential; his (reads anew P-33's exit, which he framed).

138	## 6. Where this review's evidence changes an earlier ruling
139	
140	- **J1024 §2.3 item 2, §5.1 action 3, §5.2 item 8** placed P-42's flip "inside the names batch" with the compiled tests run once before. Changed: the flip lands in 22c, because the probe measured it at one small rung with the 27 `CompilerSystem` tests passing, because row 691 shows the command as it stands miscompiles, and because phase 3's zero must be measured under the command's own setting before the phase closes.
141	- **J0929 D4, R0929 §1.1, J1023 V5 on route A:** verdicts unchanged. Changed: the ground. P-43's "Why" sentence falls (L2→L1, misdated, not his); the L1 grounds the three judgements themselves cited become the entry's reason.
142	- **J0929 F3 and J1023 on P-26:** verdict unchanged; the limit named by the exclusion brief is now a rule in the entry (layer and date), and its "unfinished text" sentence is struck.
143	- **J1024 item 1 on row 816 / P-158:** verdict unchanged; the reason sharpened: an ambiguous L1 text read by the team's own checker, with the run-time death as the cost of the other reading, not "the compiled path's way wins" alone.
144	- **J0929 item 2's option 3 (`fail: Zilch`)** is now dated (Steele 2011-06-13) and ruled not binding; R0929 §1.8's instance rule stands as the fix.
145	- **The 09-20 library-route judgement §1** ("the compiler's setting is the spec's and the interpreter's is the divergence; the reconciliation keeps the compiler's") is overruled by P-42 and by this ruling: an L1 sentence of 2009 was read as the reason for an L2 setting, against the library's practice and the later texts.
146	- **J1023 V10 and R0929 §1.7 on P-42:** unchanged; two more L1 grounds (the WD's own instantiation sentence; the 2008 text's silence) and the L2 and L3 evidence are added.
147	
148	## 7. The POSITIONS rewrites: what each new text must make the coordinator do
149	
150	Scope: the writer drafts; the trap test checks. For each entry, the behaviour the text must produce in the coordinator at a fork, in plain words. Not the text.
151	
152	- **P-26.** Make the coordinator: (1) ask which layer a ground is in before weighing it, and never let a JVM or checker limit decide what the language says; (2) rank the team's language texts by date and by consistency, with the 2019 paper last; (3) count the team's code as the team's word on the language only where the team wrote the rule on purpose (a text, a commit message, a comment, or a checker rule enforced as the language's), and never a stub by the team's own words or an accommodation of a JVM or checker gap; (4) date a code commit against the texts before calling it "later"; (5) where two later sources conflict, stop ranking and decide by P-8's goal, saying so; (6) use one word for each of the two things called specialisation. Strike the "unfinished text" sentence. Trap: a 2009 prelude commit offered as "later" than a 2011 paper; a JVM `VerifyError` offered as a reason to change a specification sentence.
153	- **P-37.** Make the coordinator: (1) carry his reason of 10-26 (no port of walk's library into the compiler's; the checker continued until it accepts the fuller library); (2) know the switch-over has two gates, the checker's zero and the code generator's zero over the thirteen, and that no library jar has yet run compiled; (3) apply ruling 3's rule when a prelude shape differs from the library's; (4) treat the prelude as a bootstrap in L2 whose shapes are evidence, not authority. Trap: a prelude stub (fixed-arity `println`) offered against the library's varargs; a checker zero offered as proof the library runs compiled.
154	- **P-43.** Make the coordinator: (1) defend the flat numbers from the exclusion rule's four texts and the WD's "mutually exclusive" sentence, never from "the prelude did it"; (2) name the prelude's flat shape as the team's compiled-world instance of the same answer; (3) weigh any return to route C against F-46 and P-95, not against a speed sentence. The two sentences of rq 219 and 220 go to history. Trap: a worker proposes `ZZ32 extends ZZ64` because "the specification's library chapter says ℤ is a subtype of ℚ".
155	- **P-42.** Make the coordinator: (1) cite POPL 2019, the WD's instantiation sentence and the library's practice as the grounds; (2) say "tuples and `()`", not "functions"; (3) know the compiled path's `Object` is one line in `Shell.java` that 22c flips, not something the switch-over ends; (4) treat Steele's 2012 setting as the compiled path's enforcement of a WD sentence on one path, not the language's rule; (5) know that `()` as a static argument and the tuple-domain dotted method fail under either bound (rows 339 and new). Trap: a worker proposes keeping `Object` "because Steele set it in 2012" or "because Java's `Object` is the top".
156	- **P-33.** Make the coordinator: (1) read phase 3's exit as the thirteen under the compile command's setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way, closed by 22c; (2) carry two zeros into phase 4; (3) place the 40 other components before P-12's step or the first program that needs each, not before the switch-over; (4) know the code generator's half was unmeasured at approval and is 52 walls now. Trap: a batch planned to clear `Avl` or `QuickCheck` before the names batch.
157	- **P-7.** Make the coordinator read "later work in the compiler" through P-26's rule, not as a rule of its own; keep the baseline sentence. Trap: as P-26's.
158	- **P-12 and P-59.** Make the coordinator: (1) size P-12's step as three pieces (the Scala checker on under walk; walk reading `CoercionInvocation`; the imported components cleared) and call it unmeasured; (2) keep walk unchanged for static-type matters until then, as J1023 V3 applied it; (3) treat "microGPT's static types are concrete" as a premise to measure when microGPT compiles. Trap: a walk rung briefed as "small" that teaches walk static coercion.
159	- **P-17 and P-84.** Make the coordinator: (1) cite `objects.tex:38` and `binary.tex:76-82` as the language's own unboxing intent beside F-11; (2) know stamping alone gives no `double[]` field and that way A4 is unmeasured; (3) hold his 09-20 class-loader lean under P-85 as a lean to confirm. Trap: a design that assumes the loader can emit a `double[]` field without a new mechanism.
160	- **P-58.** Make the coordinator: (1) say the binding form is outside the language (no foreign-function interface) and decided by the library's practice; (2) not lean on "the specification prints `builtinPrimitive`"; (3) know the choice is cheap to undo only until the bindings move. Trap: a worker proposes `import java` in the library "because the specification has no `builtinPrimitive` rule".
161	- **P-158.** Make the coordinator cite the ambiguous text, the team's checker as the team's reading, and the run-time death as the cost of the other reading. Not a rewrite of substance; one sentence.
162	
163	## 8. Defects, decisions, questions
164	
165	- **Defects found by the inputs, to route:** the tuple-domain dotted-method death (new row, section 12); row 339 confirmed; row 691 reached through row 412; F-289 to update at the flip.
166	- **Decisions of mine in this judgement:** none in the tree; the rulings above, each with its default.
167	- **Decisions not taken, for later:** `CastError` checked against the prelude's unchecked `CastException`, once row 352's `throws` check is built; the tuple-rendering device (J1024 item 14), in the names batch.
168	- **Questions for him:** section 9's list.
169	
170	## 9. For Pavol
171	
172	**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.
173	
174	**The verdict, first.**
175	
176	- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
177	- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
178	- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.
179	
180	**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.
181	
182	- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
183	- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
184	- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
185	- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
186	- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.
187	
188	**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.
189	
190	- Both happened, and the sweep finds the choice was weighed every time the two differed on a design. Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
191	- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
192	- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.
193	
194	**The decisions to take, each with a default.**
195	
196	1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. The batch's exit: the checker reports no error over those thirteen parts, under the compile command's own setting. Everything that is about generating or running code stays in phase 4. Default: yes.
197	2. **Confirm that the 40 other library parts do not block the switch-over.** They hold 624 errors. They block the later step where the interpreter runs the checker on its own programs. Each is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it. Default: yes.
198	3. **Rewrite the reasons under five entries, through the trap test you approved.** The entries: the team's later word (P-26), one library (P-37), the flat numbers (P-43), the bound (P-42), the phases (P-33), and smaller corrections to five more. The new texts must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer and date "later" correctly. You said yes to this on 26 October. Default: proceed; nothing enters until a trap test passes.
199	4. **Three one-word answers, each in your own entry.** Drop "functions" from the bound's entry, since the team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. Default: drop. Strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" from P-26; the coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike. Move the two sentences of P-43's "Why" to history and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.
200	5. **Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23.** A native is a library function whose body is Java. The decision keeps the library's own form, `builtinPrimitive("...")`, and changes only the string, to name a static Java method both paths can call. The language has no rule here, so the library's practice decides. After the 449 bindings move, the other form costs a library sweep. Default: yes, as decided.
201	6. **One lean to confirm, no decision yet.** On 20 September you leaned to the class loader as the way to store a vector of doubles as a Java `double[]`. The lean was never recorded. Record it as a lean under the array decisions, to be measured; stamping a class per type, which the loader does today, gives no `double[]` field by itself. Default: record as a lean.
202	
203	**Two things to know, no decision needed.** The probe found a compiled-path defect that does not depend on the bound: a generic method with one tuple-typed parameter dies at the call. It gets a ledger row. And the small library's cast failure is an unchecked exception where the full library's is checked; this matters only when the checker starts checking `throws` clauses, and it will come to you then.

# The foundations of the revival: the judgement

## 0. How to read this

- **The three layers**, his frame of 2026-10-26 05:25 UTC. L1, the language: the Working Draft (WD, the team's text of 2010-12, copied 2011-02-02), the revised specification, the papers of 2011, 2012 and 2019, the 2012 restart's Types chapter, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word. L2, the team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, the compiler's prelude, and walk. L3, Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer does not by itself decide a question in another. Where a team text in L1 itself argues from L2 or L3 (as the 2011 paper argues from Java), the text is the team's L1 word and its argument is theirs to make; I count it as L1.
- **Verdicts.** *Holds*: the tenet is right and its sound reason exists in the right layer. *Holds, text*: right, but its entry states a weaker, misplaced or wrong reason, or lacks the reason the coordinator needs to weigh a trade-off. *Bends*: against a team text where the team left a way the revival did not take. *Reverse*. None of the nine is a bend or a reversal.
- **Consequential** is the coordinator skill's test: reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; touches microGPT; chooses where the three principles split or are silent; or cannot be undone. A ruling so marked is his; each carries a default.

### Tenet 1. The goal and its measure (P-7, P-8). Holds.

- **Sound reason and layer.** The goal joins two layers on purpose: the intent is judged in L1 (the specification as the revival revises it, the 2012 Types chapter beside it); the measure is L2 (microGPT compiled to JVM bytecode, running fast). The language itself states the aim: the WD is "designed for producing robust high-performance software" (`philosophy.tex:14-18`, `:33-35`). P-8 is a rule of weighing, his words, and lists "the implementations" among the designers' sources: right, so long as an implementation's word is read as L2 evidence.

"Later work in the compiler" is two things: a rule the team's checker enforces on purpose (L1 intent shown in L2 code) and an accommodation of the JVM or of a checker gap (L2 only). P-7 should not restate the rule; it should point to P-26, where the distinction lives (ruling 5).
- **Risk, not defect.** The team's wind-down named a conflict between the two halves (the type system against "a virtual machine not designed to support it"), and Steele's 2016 slide 45 proposed "a less complex type system". No measurement settles it for microGPT: no compiled kernel exists, no Java baseline is written. ## 3. The prelude question: when a design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library

**The coordinator's proposal:** when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat number types; a bootstrap stub does not count.

**Ruling: right, with three sharpenings.**

1. **"Backs" is tested in L1 first.** A paper, the Types chapter, a specification sentence, a commit message or code comment that states the shape as the language's. The exclusion rule passes (four texts). The flat numbers pass through it and through the WD's "mutually exclusive".
2. **Where the L1 text is silent or ambiguous, the team's compiled checker enforcing the shape as a rule is the team's own reading of their text, and binds.** This is row 816's case: `apis.tex:252-256` reads as "no body needed" and is silent on the declaration; `source-code.tex:384-385` reads as the member declared either way; Chase's 2012 export checker counted every api member and refused a component that left one out. The run-time death (`invokeinterface` on the trait's interface) is the cost of the other reading, not the ground. So P-158 holds, and its stated reason should be this, not "by P-26, the compiled path's way wins over the interpreter's library" alone.
3. **"Later" is a date, and a stub is a stub by the team's words.** A prelude line counts as the team's later word only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. A line the team called "for now", "bogus", "bogo", "hack", "temporary", or that works around a checker gap (static arguments written at every generic call, fixed arities in place of varargs), is an accommodation and does not bind.

**Applied to the sweep.**

- **Where the revival kept the library's text against a backed prelude design: one place, row 816.** Reversed by P-158. Nothing else in the sweep's 29 rows qualifies.

## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds

**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.

**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. **What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. **The verdict, first.**

- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.

**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.

- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.

**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.

Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.

**The decisions to take, each with a default.**

1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. - Option 1 makes the zero honest before the next phase, at a cost of 4 rungs.

**Recommendation:** option 1.

Where the record does not settle something, say so and say what you would do.
+## 1. A tuple-typed parameter of a dotted method

+Climb batch 22c is running. One of its rungs makes `fortress compile` take the implicit bound `Any` in place of `Object`: one line of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java` and ten compiled tests. The rung's files are `Shell.java` and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/`. Mid-rung, its worker reports:

+"While I respelled one of the ten tests, I met the defect that the bound-`Any` probe found (`explorations/perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md`). With `object Box[\T\](x: T) first[\U\](y: (U, U)): U = do (a, c) = y; a end end`, the call `Box[\ZZ32\](1).first[\ZZ32\]((2, 3))` compiles, and the run dies at the call with `ClassCastException`. Walk prints `2`. It fails under either bound. The cause is `CodeGen.receiverPrependedDomainType` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6250-6263`), which cannot tell one parameter of a tuple type from several parameters. The team's comment at that site reads: 'I think we start to have a problem here in the future, when generics can be parametrized by tuples. We need to figure out what this means.'
+I see two ways, and I lean to the first.

+(a) Make the shape a static error of the language. The type group, who built the compiled path, left it unsettled. P-26 says that they worked to make the language run and learned what is feasible, and that the implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. P-77 already makes a limit of the JVM a rule of the language. So the checker, and walk's load check, refuse a generic method called with a dot whose one parameter has a tuple type; a revision callout in `Specification/basic/functions.tex` states the rule and its reason, as P-95 asks; and the new ledger row is classed `design limit (specification)`. About 20 lines. No declaration of the library has the shape.

+(b) Keep the compiled path's extends-`Object` pre-desugaring for the static parameters of dotted methods only. The Working Draft gives a type parameter with no `extends` clause the bound `Object` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:50`), and an `Object` bound keeps tuple static arguments out of such methods.
+A fix in the code generator is outside my files, and I cannot size it."

+{POSITIONS 42}
+{POSITIONS 77}

+## 2. The order traits' self type, in a planner's draft

+The planner's draft record for climb batch 22c, the batch that closes phase 3, holds a rung that none of its other rungs needs. The rung rests on a sweep of the record against the compiler's prelude, which reports:

+- The compiler's prelude spells the order traits with the self-type idiom, and with no F-bound: `trait StandardTotalOrder[\T\] extends {Equality[\T\], AllStandardTotalOrders} comprises T` and `trait Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`).

+- The team's last edits of `StandardTotalOrder` are Guy Steele's of June 2012. On 2012-06-05 (`655e65d53`) he added `comprises T` to the F-bounded `trait StandardTotalOrder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]`. On 2012-06-06 (`59fdeff62`) he took the F-bound away, in the same commit as a change of the checker for `comprises` clauses. So on the compiled path, the team's last word on this trait went from the F-bound, which the interpreter's library still has, to the idiom.
+- The history of the idiom in the notes behind P-146 stops at 2011-12-06 (`explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-ways.md`, section 3, step 7). Those notes call the idiom way 5.

+The rung is way 5: `comprises T` on the seven traits of the interpreter's library that way 5 names in `explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md`, after walk's six-line edit of `BuildEnvironments.finishTrait`, so that walk does not overflow its stack on the clause (row 407). +"The checker's `case` rule for a clause with no comparison operator chooses ∈ or `=` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:1396-1403`. In the compiler's world, it asks whether the guard's type is a subtype of `GeneratorZZ32`, the prelude's range trait (`Types.makeGeneratorZZ32Type`; `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:111`). In the one-library world, a branch that the revival added asks whether a trait type has `Contains` among its ancestors, and answers false for every other type. So a guard typed by a type variable bounded by `Range[\ZZ32\]`, or by a union of ranges, gets `=`, and the clause never matches. I see two ways.

+(a) The prelude's way. Declare `trait GeneratorZZ32` in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, make the scalar `ZZ32` ranges extend it, and let both worlds ask the team's question, the subtype test against `GeneratorZZ32`. The revival's branch goes. A subtype test sees through a type variable's bound and through a union, so row 480 closes. Two library lines, and a deletion in the checker.

+(b) Row 480's own fix. Keep the question about `Contains`, and answer it for a type variable through its bounds, for a union through all its members, and for an intersection through any of them. About 15 lines of the checker; no library line.

P-77 already takes the prelude's `ZZ32` ranges, as the prelude declares them. And (a) is the team's own checker code."

<!-- The key to the four trap scenarios of questions.md, written from today's POSITIONS entries and the curator's words of 2026-10-25 and 2026-10-26, before any rewrite of P-26 or P-37 existed: for each scenario the right decision and its grounds, the wrong decision that today's text invites and the sentence that invites it, and the record-test kit's rubric. -->

# Trap test: the key

For the grader. Two readers answered `questions.md` as the coordinating session, each in its own copy of the repository. One copy holds today's POSITIONS entries. The other holds the rewritten ones, with today's texts moved to `POSITIONS-history.md`. You score blind to the copy. For each scenario this key gives the right decision and its reasons; the curator's words that it rests on; the wrong decision that today's entries invite, with the sentences that invite it; the facts it rests on and where each lives; other wrong answers; and the rubric.

Paths are under `explorations/` unless they start with `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/`, `Specification/`, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, `Papers/` or `.claude/`. "Row N" is a gap-ledger row (`coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger:N'`). "The coordinator skill" is `.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md`.

**Scoring** (the kit's rubric, `coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/key.md`). **Decision 0-2**: 2, the decision is right and rests on the facts below; 1, right in the main but missing a fact that changes a step or a ground; 0, wrong, or a step that cannot work, or a decision of the curator's contradicted, or a re-measurement of what the record holds. **Sources 0-1**: 1, every load-bearing fact beyond the quoted entries is cited to a source that holds it (the sources below, or an equivalent one), or the answer needed none; 0, such a fact is asserted without a source, invented, or the answer stops at the quoted entries where they could not carry it.

A reader who reaches the right decision by a ground in the wrong layer (below, his words of 05:25) gets at most 1 for the decision: the test is whether the record orients the coordinator's judgement, not only its verdict.

## The curator's words that the key rests on

UTC, 2026-10-25 and 2026-10-26, cleaned of dictation slips. The transcript holds them; `coordinator/POSITIONS-history.md` holds the one of 04:28 under P-158.

1. **The three layers** (10-26 05:25): what Fortress does, against how Fortress is implemented on the JVM, and, related, interoperability with Java. The rule drawn from them (the coordinator's wording of 07:38, to which he said yes at 07:42): a ground from one layer does not decide a question in another. A sentence of the specification is not by itself the reason for a setting of the compiled path, and an implementation limit is not by itself a rule of the language.

## 4. `System` on the compiled path after the switch-over

**The right decision.**

- **The rung does not go in as drafted.** It keeps a compiler-only copy of a library component, `CompilerSystem`, as the compiled path's `System`, and ports walk's declarations into it. That is the porting that the switch-over exists to avoid. The api name `System` would mean two components, one per path, as `WellKnownNames` re-points the prelude today, the team's "Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java:115`). And `args` would have two types: a `StringVector` on the compiled path, the prelude's hand-written Java class that the specification does not have (F-183), and an `ImmutableArray[\String,ZZ32\]` under walk (`Library/System.fsi`).

# Fortress revival

Fortress was an experimental programming language from Sun Labs (2003–2012).
This repository revives it: the goal is to finish the original team's design,
judged by its specification (`Specification/`) and its type research
(`Papers/`), and measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and
running fast.

## Where your training applies, and where it does not

- Known languages: the interpreter, the code generator and the run time are
  Java (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`); the static type checker is
  Scala (`.../scala_src/`); the parser grammars are Rats! (`.../parser/*.rats`);
  the syntax tree is generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`; the
  build is Ant; the specification and the papers are LaTeX.
- Fortress itself: the library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`),
  the tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`, `compiler_tests/` and the other test
  folders) and every `.fss` and `.fsi` file. Fortress is not in your training
  in any depth. It looks like Scala in places, and its library's algebraic
  traits recall Haskell's numeric classes, but its rules differ (multiple
  dispatch, juxtaposition as an operator, loops parallel by default), so
  assuming it behaves like a language you know can lead you astray.

## How to work here

- Before any build, test run, edit, measurement, commit or agent launch, load
  the `fortress-repo` skill, which also covers long commands and waits; for
  the cloud container's machine, disk, stops and restarts, and a lost
  container, the `cloud-container` skill.
- The coordinating session loads the `fortress-repo` skill, then the
  `coordinator` skill, at session start and after every compaction, and boots
  and works by the `coordinator` skill, which also covers running agents and
  resuming runs.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/coordinator

# The coordinating session

You talk to the curator, brief the workers and keep the record. Load a part under `references/` when you switch into its work.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**worker**
: Agent that you launch for one task: an Agent-tool subagent, a Workflow agent or a headless `claude -p` session.

**record**
: Project's memory, kept in the repository: the files that the core lists below.

**entry**
: Line of `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md` under its permanent number, such as `F-87` or `P-48`.

**PLAN**
: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its phases end with 3, the distance at zero (`references/batch.md`); 4, the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.

**review queue**
: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, the one home of each item that waits for the curator's word or review, numbered and sorted by theme. A pointer cites an item by its number.

**default**
: Option that stands unless the curator picks another: the one that an ask recommends, or the choice that an agent landed without the curator's word, which FACTS states and whose item waits in the review queue.

**batch**
: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.

**rung**
: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.

**fork**
: Design question with more than one way forward.

**cross-area question**
: Fork that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation.

**go**
: Curator's approval to start a named piece of work. A bare go, "go" with nothing named, starts the background work that you proposed, never a batch. A standing go covers a named series of work, and stands in this skill.

**ask**
: Message that puts one decision to the curator.

**hold**
: Decision that the work waits on until the curator answers.

**review list**
: PLAN's list "listed for his review" under each batch: one line for each item for the curator's later review, with a pointer to its item in the review queue once the queue holds it.

**interrupt**
: Stop of a turn by the stop button.

**process stop**
: End of the session's process, by the platform's cap, idleness or a VM restart. The platform restarts it in the same session.

**tokens written**
: Input tokens and tokens written to the prompt cache, as `explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py` counts them.

**boot note**
: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, what is in flight now.

**held list**
: `explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, the points that the curator raised while reading, one line each.

**model check**
: Stop hook `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, which raises an alarm after a turn of the coordinating session that ran on neither Opus nor Fable.

**git-check switch**
: Hook `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, which keeps the platform's git-check hook off.

## The standing goal

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows and source to workers. Read a worker's final report yourself.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.

## The facts of this environment

- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
- A process stop comes about every 13 hours. Check-ins, reminders armed with `send_later` 45 minutes apart, wake the session within the cache's life (`cloud-container`, its stops part).
- A message that the curator sends during a turn is queued. An interrupt kills every running agent.
- The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part). Its reminders are advisory. If a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn: answer it as "Quiet times" says.
- Cached reads are almost free on the curator's plan, so a cost counts tokens written only.
- A worker runs on Opus unless `references/delegating.md` names another tier. Sonnet writes nothing that the curator reads.
- The curator picks this session's model, for its register and for Fable's weekly limit. The boot note names it.

## Talking to the curator

- Write plain short sentences, with contractions, halfway to ASD-STE100: active voice, one word for one thing. Keep replies brief.
- Give advice as instructions, in literal words. Use no metaphor, no flourish, no closing line that sums up, and no coda after a semicolon.
- Use no internal shorthand. Define a term that is new to the curator where you use it, even a common term of the work, such as reshape, outer product, Ring or matrix multiplication.
- Never quote an entry's bold title as the curator's words. It is the record's handle.
- Use lists, not tables. The iOS client shows a table as one line that scrolls sideways.
- Write numbers as K or M: 5K, 1.2M. Give few, each with its meaning.
- Read the clock before you write any time, in a call of its own. Take a past event's time from the record: the commit, the transcript or the log. Give a time in UTC and in the curator's time. Never place an event from feel, such as "yesterday".
- Give estimates in the project's units, such as rungs, never in days. Give costs in tokens written, never in dollars.
- Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool: its prompt times out after about 60 seconds in the iOS client. If that timeout ends, the rule lapses.
- Put every result in the turn's final text, never between tool calls. The client folds text between tool calls out of view.
- If you think the curator is wrong, say so and show why.
- Once after each boot, at the first explanation or ask, read `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/PROFILE.md` (about 9K characters). It grades by topic what the curator knows: pitch each topic at its level. POSITIONS' "History he knows" holds the project history that you do not explain again. Where the two disagree, POSITIONS rules: fix the profile.

**An ask.** Put decisions one at a time, one ask in a message, in this order:

1. The question, in one line.
2. The context, in short bullets. Start with a short primer in plain words, with a Fortress example. Say why the design exists. Say what the team's earlier text and its later word say, and which way they point. Then give the library's own way, and how to judge the fork. Give what the peers do as context. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.

Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.

Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.

**Quiet times.**

- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.

  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.

**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.

- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.

**Pages.**

- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.

## The record: what goes where

Under `explorations/coordinator/`:

- `FACTS.md`: what is true of the project now.
- `POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions about the project.
- `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`: each entry's provenance and earlier lines.
- `INDEX.md`: one line for each note.
- `PLAN.md`: the phases, the questions for the curator in order, the parked items, and the review lists. Its first section says where the work stands.
- `PLAN-history.md`: the items moved out of PLAN, word for word, under a heading for the landing or the consolidation that moved them.
- The boot note, the one home of state: what runs, with each run's ID and estimate; what to do when it ends; a question waiting on the curator; the session's model; the one next process stop; the armed check-ins, by name; and the URLs of live pages. During a batch, the run's ID and the check-ins' IDs are in the check-in file that the boot note names (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- The held list. Its last section holds the smaller items that the curator owns.
- `review-queue.md`: the review queue.

Elsewhere: the reports and notes, which hold the detail; the gap ledger, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, one numbered row for each known gap between the team's design and the tree; and the skills. This skill holds how you work with the curator and the workers. `fortress-repo` holds the rules that bind workers. `cloud-container` holds the platform.

FACTS and POSITIONS hold the project only, since briefs quote them. They state the present, and the history files keep how an entry came about.

- Search the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`: `'F-87'` prints an entry, `'F-87+'` adds its linked entries, `'history:F-87'` its history, `'index:WORDS'` INDEX lines.
- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py` (`references/record.md`).
- Keep one home for each thing, and point to it from elsewhere.
- Have the skill writer (`references/skill-rewrite.md`) put each rule that the curator states about your work into its skill. Keep it on the held list until then.
- Commit only the paths that you name. Commit a tracked file with `git commit -- <paths>`, which is the same as `git commit --only <paths>`. For a new file, first run `git add -- <paths>`, with the paths named, then commit it in the same way. Never use `git add -A`, `git add .` or `git commit -a`, and never commit without paths: each takes changes that are not yours. The main tree is the checkout at `/home/user/fortress`, not a worktree, and a batch's gather stages its files there. While a batch runs, edit nothing tracked there (`references/batch.md`, "While it runs").
- Push after every commit, in the order of `fortress-repo`'s committing part.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order:

0. Check the serving model with the `get_session` tool and no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If either field names a model other than Opus or Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below).
1. `CLAUDE.md`, then this file.
2. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
3. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
5. The boot note, then the held list.
6. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.

**A light boot.** When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0, 1 and 4 to 7, and skip steps 2 and 3: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. Then read the parts of the skills that the work in hand touches, as the boot note names them, if it does. Before you state a fact or a decision, or put anything to the curator, search the record with `facts-extract.sh`. The full boot is the default. The curator's word for a light boot replaces the hook's list of files after a compaction.

- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
  - do no other work until `get_session` shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.

  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could no
