- F-67 **The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters.** A size is a size parameter's name, a literal or an operation on sizes. Two sizes are equal when their written forms are, once each operation on numerals is computed, so `2 3` equals `6` but `m n` does not equal `n m` (F-146). The checker refuses to infer a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` static argument (`XXXNatBoolChecker`). It does not compare `bool` arguments, so `object F extends { Flag[\true\], Flag[\false\] }`, two instantiations of one trait, passes it, and code generation then stops on it (row 406, open, a part of P-40 still to build). A call that leaves a size unknown is refused, "Could not infer static argument ... without context"; F-69 gives when an overload set is refused and when it is not. It builds P-40. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatInferredChecker`, `NatWrittenChecker`, `NatMethodChecker`, `NatExportChecker` and `XXXNatMismatchChecker`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-68 **The checker's return-type rule reads a size as it reads a type parameter.** A size of the less specific declaration that the domains leave unsolved stays that declaration's own parameter, as `Papers/Types/overloading-check.tick` binds `Δ2`. So an override returning `Dn[\T,3,s\]` over `Up[\T,b,s\]` is refused, like its type-parameter twin, and the library's `subarray` override passes. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatOverrideChecker` and `XXXNatRetSizeChecker`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-69 **The compiled checker refuses a call whose most specific arm failed only on a size that the call cannot fix, when that arm's parameter types are free of the size.** The message is "Could not infer static argument nat n without context". It drops instead an arm whose unknown size is in its own parameter types (row 400, open). It lets through a call whose argument's static type lies above the arm's domain, and the compiled run dies reading the size (row 446, open). It builds P-40. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatKnownSizeArm`, which compiles and runs a call that fixes the size, and `XXXNatUnknownSize*`, which pin the refusal's message; rows 400 and 446 have no test. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-unknown-size-arm/REPORT.md` section 10.
- F-70 **The compiled checker checks a static argument written at a dotted method call against its parameter's bound, but not one written at a top-level function call.** At a dotted call it puts the written arguments into each bound and refuses a call whose argument misses one, "No such method" (row 651, fixed). At a top-level call it matches kinds only, so `n[\String\]("d")` passes for `n[\T extends Number\](s: String): T` (row 470, open). Gated by `compiler_tests/MethodStaticArgsBoundNamesOther*`, which accept a dotted call whose written arguments meet their bounds. No test pins the refusal of an argument that misses its bound; a probe showed it (`rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md` section 6). Row 470 can have no gated test, since the harness has no form for a program that the specification refuses and the checker accepts. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-contexts/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-71 **The compiled checker does not narrow the variable of the shorthand form `typecase x of T => ...`, neither path accepts the binding form `typecase x = e of`, and the clause-binding form `typecase e of y: T => ... end` runs on both paths.** So write the clause-binding form, as the library does (F-134): its `cast` writes `typecase x of x':T => x' ... end`. In the shorthand form, the checker refuses a clause that uses `x` as a `T`, and such a clause runs under walk only; a clause that does not, as in the library's `instanceOf`, passes. The binding form parses as the equality `x = e`. Only the specification's grammar has it, under the team's note that the section awaits the pattern-matching proposal (`typecase.tex:15`). Row 460 records both refusals, and no test gates them. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-exclusion-remainder/REPORT.md` section 15.
- F-72 **The compiled checker reads a `comprises` clause for a generic subtrait as the team's 2012 texts do (Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight; P-44): the subtrait may extend the closed trait when the trait table knows at least one type that immediately extends the subtrait, and each such type is below a listed type.** It builds P-44. This rule leaves the ellipsis refusal of F-64 (row 354, open) as it was. Open: an extender in another compilation unit escapes the check, the hole that P-44 leaves (row 487). The verdict changes when the extender renames its type variable (row 489), and the extenders are found by the simple text of the trait's name (row 490). Gated by `compiler_tests/ComprisesGenericSubtrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-comprises-checker/REPORT.md` section 6.
- F-73 **The compiled checker infers a generic's static arguments with coercion: a type parameter that is the whole type of each parameter it occurs in, as `T` in `pick[\T\](x: T, y: T)`, takes the narrowest type that every one of its arguments converts into and its bound permits.** It looks for that type among its arguments' types, their coercion targets and its bound, the bound only when it is a trait type other than `Object` or `Any`. It builds P-74 and P-49. A coerced declaration ranks below one that needs no coercion. A tie among coerced declarations is refused, "Ambiguous coercion", outside three narrow cases (the report's section 3.2). When the tied declarations differ only at positions where the call passes a numeral, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit; that reading is a default. The coercion attempt refuses a call beyond 64 combinations of candidate types (row 506) and a call with an untyped function argument (row 507). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatLitArgChecker`, `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` and `InferCoercionShapes`, which F-51 also cites, and the refusal of a tie by `XXXInferAmbiguousCoercion`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-inference-checker/REPORT.md` section 3.2.
- F-74 **Under walk, an integer numeral takes its type from its value: a `ZZ32` if it fits 32 bits, a `ZZ64` if it fits 64 bits, a `ZZ` above that; it stays so until walk has the checker's static types, since without them a list of numerals and a generic's static argument take their types from the values.** Its run-time type is the library's value object `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum`, below `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:125`, `:128`, `:223`). Walk instantiates a generic at it, so a `Box[\Int\]` is a type apart from `Box[\ZZ32\]` and dispatches past it (row 364). F-74 is why P-76's walk half waits; F-79 is the library half, built. Probe Q (`compile-ladder/plan-n/probe-q/PROBE-Q.md`) measured walk with every integer numeral an `IntLiteral`, the numeral's own type in the library. It ran before climb batch N's second run and before the library half landed. Alone, the switch changed 59 test verdicts. With four devices (a numeral at an `AnyIntegral` parameter read as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, a tuple of numerals converted at dispatch, `asif` converting, a varargs list converted at dispatch), the library loaded and both microGPT checks kept their values, but 24 passing interpreter tests failed: 6 by design, 3 of them team tests that assert a `ZZ32`; 9 for want of static types (rows 364, 510); and 9 walk gaps. A size used as a value is a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and a `ZZ64` above (row 486; F-140). Detail: `reviews/numeral-switch-judgement.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-75 **The compiled checker checks the Return Type Rule over every instance, and a positional rule: when two generic declarations in the more-specific relation declare as many static parameters of their own, those parameters agree in kind by position, and the more specific return type is a subtype of the other once the other's parameters are read as its own by position.** The equal-count scope and the comparison of kinds are the rung's choices. It builds P-45. Checking every instance, as P-45 asks, it also refuses a generic declaration beside a plain one whose domain is an object type, a pair that the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`) accepts, since the paper sets aside the instances whose domains cannot meet (row 542, open). In the interpreter's library the two rules refuse no pair: the distance holds no return-type or overloading error (F-53). Gated by `compiler_tests/OverloadGeneric*` and `OverloadBoundNamesForced`, which accept; `XXXOverloadReturnEveryInstance` and `XXXOverloadPermutedStaticParams`, which pin the two rules' refusals; and `XXXOverloadReturnObjectDomain`, which pins row 542's. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/decision-record.md` sections 1 and 2.
- F-76 **The compiled checker accepts the specification's `comprises` example of the Meet Rule (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "The Meet Rule for Functions") by a coverage check used only in overload checking, not in its subtype test, and types a call whose argument's static type lies below closed traits and above the types that they list by the intersection of the return types of its most specific declarations, when they tie without coercion.** It builds P-60, which reads `comprises` at the level of values: several declarations below two overloads serve as their meet if together they cover it. Open: coverage refuses a pair when a declaration that it compares has static parameters (row 546). In an accepted family that has any other generic declaration, such a call is typed by the head of a sort, which follows declaration order and can vary between runs, not by the intersection (row 543). That narrower scope than P-60's is a default. On the compiled path, a method call on a value typed by the intersection crashes the code generator (row 540), and a generic declaration instantiated at an intersection type dies as it loads (row 559). The checker checks a `comprises` clause only at the closed trait's immediate subtypes, so a type in another component below a generic subtrait escapes it (row 487). Its verdict on an overload set can depend on the components compiled before it in the same JVM (row 547). Gated by `compiler_tests/*Comprises*` and `*CoverageReturn*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-return-type-rule/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-77 **The one library repairs its refused overload families with its own exclusions, and the checker accepts its `seq` pairs by the rule for functional methods (F-80).** It builds P-45. `StandardMin`, `StandardMax`, `SequentialGenerator` and `FilterGenerator` exclude `HasRank`, `String` excludes `AnyMultiplicativeRing`, and `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax` (P-98). Marker traits instead would give two ordered types several minimal common supertypes, which walk mishandles (rows 555, 589). Gated by `tests/LibraryOverloadFamilies.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overload-families/REPORT.md` section 4.
- F-78 **The compiled checker instantiates a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes at the intersection of its upper bounds, never `BottomType`, and tries a call by subtyping without the expected type first.** It builds P-48 and P-49. Where the call has an expected type, its attempts come in this order: subtyping without the expected type, kept when its result converts to it; subtyping with the expected type; coercion with it; and coercion without it. The second lets a call whose untyped function argument only the expected type fixes type-check, since the coercion attempt cannot check such an argument (row 507). P-49 decides the first and the third; the second and the fourth are an agent's choice, the instance-bound rung's (its decision record, D4). An argument of intersection type fixes a parameter at the whole intersection, not at one conjunct (row 541). The run time has no class for an intersection type, so such an instance dies as it loads (row 559). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferResultOnly*` and `InferContextKeepsFit`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 7; the order, by reading, `compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md`, D4, and `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:733-737`.
- F-79 **In the interpreter's library, `IntLiteral`, the type that the compiled checker gives an integer numeral, is declared on the model of the compiler's prelude: a sibling of the number types under `Number`, which each integer type, `QQ`, `RR64` and `AnyIntegral` convert from by coercion.** It builds the library half of P-76. Under walk a numeral is still a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, so no numeral reaches these declarations until walk's half is built (F-74). `IntLiteral` declares itself the members of `Integral[\I\]` that a numeral could not reach, among them the getters `zero` and `one`, `odd`, `even`, `floor` and `DIVIDES`. There are three reasons: for some, no declaration of `Integral` applies to a sibling type even with coercion; for others, the declarations that apply by coercion tie; and a getter must be the type's own member. Each integer type declares its own comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and a `^` with an `IntLiteral` exponent. Without them, a typed integer with a numeral operand ties between a declaration inherited from a generic trait and the same operator's own declarations in `ZZ64`, `QQ` and `RR64`. The compiled checker refuses `(3).minimum` and `(3).maximum`, `ZZ32`'s getters (row 581). Gated under walk by `tests/IntegerOrderNumerals.fss`, which checks each integer type's own comparisons, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-library/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 6.
- F-80 **The compiled checker judges two functional methods of one name, abstract declarations included, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in each type that provides both.** Such a type must provide their meet, compared without the `self` parameter. F-88 says what a type provides. An abstract functional method beside a concrete one in the same trait, with the same parameter types, is refused by the No Duplicates Rule. Unchecked: a pair that only an object expression provides (row 570). It checks every operator, a symbol such as `+`, `<`, `||` or a subscript as well as a name of capitals such as `CAP` or a word such as `juxtaposition` (F-281). The checker's overloading memo is keyed on all the inputs of the check, so a pair accepted at the top level is not reused unchecked in a trait that provides it. Gated by `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodMeet*`, and by the refusals that the specification asks for, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetAbstractSibling`, `XXXNoDuplicatesRuleAbstract` and, for an operator, `XXXFunctionalMethodMeetOperatorChecker`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` sections 5 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-81 **In the interpreter's library, every Meet Rule pair inside one type that the compiled checker checks has a declaration on its meet, and the checker checks every operator (F-281).** `String`'s juxtaposition is three top-level operators, since two functional methods with `self` at different positions have no meet. `String`'s `||`, `|||`, `//` and `///`, which paired `(a:Any, self)` with `(self, b:Any)`, the shape the specification refuses, are now three top-level operators each too (F-276). F-245's measurement found other invalid pairs, among them `Indexed`'s three subscripts in 17 types, valid since the index bound (F-278). The rung that added these meets also set the declared types listed in report section 1 to what their bodies answer. `__bigOperator2`'s fused branch, whose arm's type the `typecase` cannot show, casts its result to the declared `O0` (F-85). Gated by `tests/LibraryMeetDeclarations.fss`, and for the symbolic operators by the distance stage, which finds no overloading error in the library (F-245). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-meets/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-82 **In the interpreter's library, the range types declare a method on the meet for each of their Meet Rule pairs that the compiled checker checks, and their declared types match what their bodies answer.** Among the meets are `CAP` at each rank, a range's number of dimensions (F-89 holds the ranks' kinds), and `FullRange`'s abstract `IN`, so a numeral `IN` a `#` or `:` range type-checks (row 580, fixed). - F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and the exclusion test reads its signatures plain. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` dies at class load with a `VerifyError` when the trait's self-type parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]`: an open defect (row 695). The rule refuses, rightly, a team declaration, `PureList`'s `List` (row 355); the demo `trips.fss`'s `generator`, which it refused, extends `StandardTotalOrder[\generator\]` since its repair (row 710; `ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss:96`). The same function builds the methods that a trait's body sees, so a call of an inherited method by its bare name inside a trait gets the same renaming. 1	<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->
2	
3	# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground
4	
5	## The goal
6	
7	- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
8	- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
9	- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what microGPT invented goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
10	- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
11	- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
12	- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).
13	
14	## History he knows (do not re-explain)
15	
16	- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
17	- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.
18	
19	## Decisions on record
20	
21	### The standard and the sources
22	
23	- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it (P-26: the specification is revised to the team's later word). Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
24	- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper (F-166). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
25	- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
26	- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
27	- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
28	- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
29	- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
30	- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3, the compiled checker reports no error on the interpreter's whole library (the distance to the switch-over at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value); phase 4, the switch-over, first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.
31	
32	### The one library and the compiled checker
33	
34	- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).
35	- P-38 **The compiler prelude's defects are not repaired: they go with it at the switch-over.** Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
36	- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. The gates of batches whose work drives the distance down also measure the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the distance's full measurement takes far longer than the count, and a batch pays for it only when the distance is the number that it tries to move.
37	- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
38	- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
39	- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`, and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412).
40	- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
41	- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, whose `where` form is not built. `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check of 2012 enforces it; by P-26, on the team's later word, that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification asks for no body there, not for no declaration (`Specification/basic/components/apis.tex`, "Component and API Identity"). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).
70	
71	### Numbers
72	
73	- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
74	- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** Under walk and on the compiled path, `round(2.5)` gives 2: an `RR64` or `RR32` value rounds an exact half to the even integer, as a rational does. This is the specification's rule for rationals, the default rounding of IEEE 754, and the rule of the team's own `round` on rationals.
75	- P-68 **On the float types, `floor` and `ceiling` return the same float type, while the brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ`, the unbounded integer.** So `floor(2.5)` is the `RR64` value 2.0, and ⌊2.5⌋ is to be the `ZZ` value 2. Row 330: one library rung after the switch-over, which first counts the interpreter tests whose output changes, then makes the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return `ZZ` in each of the library's declarations of them; today the brackets are `ZZ64` under walk and `RR64` compiled, and `round` and `truncate` are `ZZ64`, `ZZ` or `RR64` by declaration.
76	- P-69 **`LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are bit operators on the fixed-width integer types, and `ZZ`'s `shift` is exact.** On `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, a shift loses the bits that it shifts out, silently, as in every peer language. A count at or beyond the width gives 0, or -1 for `RSHIFT` of a negative value, and a negative count shifts the other way, as Swift's and Julia's shifts do. The count may have any integer type, and the shift works at the width of the value shifted. On `ZZ`, the unbounded integers ℤ, `shift(x, k)` is ⌊x·2^k⌋ at any count; there the specification defines `x LSHIFT k` as `shift(x, k)` and `x RSHIFT k` as `shift(x, -k)`. On the compiled path, a shift of a fixed-width value works on the JVM's `int` or `long`, never through `ZZ`. Why: a shift through `ZZ` costs speed wherever the JVM cannot remove it. Row 442: the compiled `NN32` and `NN64` shifts, refused today. Row 383: `ZZ`'s `shift`, which the compiler's prelude does not declare. Row 381: a count of another integer type, where the compiled path refuses a `ZZ`, `NN32` or `NN64` count and computes a `ZZ64` count on a `ZZ32` at 64 bits.
77	- P-70 **`GCD` and `LCM` give nonnegative results, and `LCM` raises `IntegerOverflow` when the multiple does not fit its type.** So `0 GCD -4` is 4 and `1 LCM -5` is 5, and on `ZZ32`, `(2^31 - 1) LCM 2` raises. The rule applies on both paths. Why: the specification says that both results are nonnegative, and its general rule raises `IntegerOverflow` for an integer result that does not fit. The same general rule makes `GCD` raise it where the divisor does not fit, as in the specification's example `-2^31 GCD 0` on `ZZ32`. Row 442: `GCD` and `LCM` on the compiled path's `NN32` and `NN64`.
78	- P-71 **An overflow guard tests for the type's most negative value, not for `a = -a`, so `|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow.** On a signed fixed-width type, only the most negative value overflows when it is negated, taken in absolute value or divided by -1. The test `a = -a` is true for that value, and also for 0. Walk already gave 0 in the three cases. On the compiled path, the natives of negation, absolute value and division on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` test for the most negative value. The same faulty test sat in `ZZ64`'s multiplication, through which its `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD` and `LCM` compute, so `0 · 5`, `3 REM 5` and `12 GCD 18` raised; that multiplication now raises only when the exact product does not fit. Why: no reading of the specification makes the three cases overflow.
79	- P-72 **`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits of a value that the narrower type cannot hold, signed and unsigned, on both paths, and raises no `IntegerOverflow`.** The decision covers `narrow` from a `ZZ64` to a `ZZ32` and from an `NN64` to an `NN32`. A value that the narrower type holds is unchanged; any other becomes the value of the narrower type with the same low 32 bits. Why: the team's specification said nothing on `narrow`, and the team's boundary test `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts the low 32 bits for `NN64` values. On the unsigned types, keeping the low bits is a bit operation, like a shift, and the signed `narrow` gets the same answer.
80	- P-73 **Under walk, fixed-width integer arithmetic raises `IntegerOverflow` when its result does not fit, on the unsigned `NN32` and `NN64` too.** The rule covers every operation whose result can leave its type, `^`, `CHOOSE` and `LCM` included (F-132 holds what is built and its tests). So a subtraction below 0 on `NN32` raises. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators ∔ (`DOTPLUS`), ∸ (`DOTMINUS`) and ⨰ (`DOTTIMES`), fully parenthesised, since the specification states their precedence only among the three. The specification's saturating operators, such as ⊞ (`BOXPLUS`), are not in the interpreter's library; they come in a later step of their own (row 797). Why: this is the specification's rule, and the compiled path already raised the error for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, negation and absolute value on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`. The decision is walk's. On the compiled path the rule holds as the specification's (P-25, the standard), and the compiled path departs from it at `^` (rows 523 to 525) and at `CHOOSE` (row 521).
81	- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.
82	- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64` implicitly, since every `NN32` value converts to `RR64` exactly.** Why: a conversion that fits is implicit, the rule of P-74 on mixed widths. With the coercion, an operator that both `RR64` and `ZZ64` declare is ambiguous on both paths for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32`, since neither `ZZ64` nor `RR64` coerces into the other. Without it, P-74's rule, the narrowest type into which both arguments coerce, gives `ZZ64`. Row 575: the coercion, which the tree lacks, with this conflict and its measurement. Each way to build it changes a decided behaviour, so the choice of a way is not a worker's (`fortress-repo`'s exploring part).
83	- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32` in a `typecase` or an overload (row 79), a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), an integer numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
84	- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.
85	- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.
86	- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known: the five demos that walk refuses at load, since they leave an inherited abstract method without a body (row 670, which names them); `trips.fss`, which walk runs but the compiled checker refuses, since its `generator` object extends `StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` without being a `trip` (row 710); the timing line of `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, which divides a `ZZ64` by a float and so stops walk (row 791); and the reductions that the compiled checker refuses because they leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
87	- P-80 **The specification's sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset of a type at run time.** These types are the specification's subtypes by sign, such as positive ℚ, non-negative ℚ and non-zero ℚ, and the same refinements of the integers. The machine types `NN32` and `NN64` are separate types, not among them. The specification's number chapters now test a value's sign by comparison, and a float with two getters of `RR64`: `check` returns `Just(x)` for a finite `x`, `check_star` returns `Just(x)` for an `x` that is not a NaN, and each returns `Nothing` otherwise. The chapter that held the design, `Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex`, stays word for word, marked superseded by a callout in the form of every specification change (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Their possible return belongs to P-62: once the `covariant` keyword is built, a worker tries to bring them back as covariant static parameters.
88	- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
89	
90	### Arrays and the model program
91	
92	- P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).
93	- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.
94	- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** The model is microGPT's two programs; the vocabulary is the array operations that they are written in (`FlatArrays.fss` for C4, the flat program, and `FlatArrays2.fss` for the APL-style one). No operator in the model is replaced by a function call to pass an overload check, as a proposed repair once wrote `planeSum(mask, x)` for `mask + x`; the vocabulary changes instead. Any repair that changes a line of the model is shown to the curator as a diff before it is built. Decision D, still open and returning after the switch-over with the other array decisions (P-85), is such a diff: it gives C4's arrays sized types, in its vocabulary's signatures and in the model lines that these force (`explorations/reviews/decision-d-diff.md`; the patch itself is only in git, in the parent of `84aef6a4f`). Nothing of decision D is applied before microGPT compiles, after the switch-over.
95	- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
96	- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
97	- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
98	- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.
99	
100	### The specification's revision
101	
102	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
103	- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
104	- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
105	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.
106	
107	### The suites and the gate
108	
109	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
110	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
111	- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
112	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
113	- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what microGPT invented goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. 25

27	2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). Chase's 2012 export check (`5a68404fd`) enforced it: a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
28	3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, Chase's check refused 12 such members. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.
112	
113	**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. No team text says the code generator, class loader or RTTI needs `Object` (archaeology §2.6, §5). The code reads the other way: Naden's dispatcher ignores a written `Any` bound as "meaningless" and checks any other (`OverloadSet.java:1516-1517`); `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` names an empty clause `Object` only in a generic method's name, which declaration and call compute alike. The team's texts after 2012-05-30 (Types, 05-31; Naden, 08-31; POPL 2019) do not carry `Object` as the default. So the setting is the compiled path's departure from the language's rule, L2, and ends by one line.
114	
115	**L2, the probe.** Under `Any`, generic functions, objects, traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase` at a pair or an arrow compile, load and run, making the same classes and the same bytecode as with `extends Any` written; the 23 `CompilerSystem` `.test` files pass under both settings; `ant testQuick` under `Any` gives 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side (one promotion, three pinned texts, four `where [\E extends Object\]` workarounds of row 412, one premise, one prelude limit). Under `Object`, `q = id((3, 4))` compiles and runs `id(3)`, printing `q + 1 = 4` (row 691 reached by row 412): the compile command as it stands can silently miscompile. `()` dies under either bound (row 339, confirmed by `javap`); a generic dotted method with a single tuple-typed parameter dies under either bound (new, `CodeGen.java:6250-6263`, the team's comment "when generics can be parametrized by tuples"). Neither depends on the bound.
116	
117	**L3.** `java.lang.Object` is translated to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`); natives are written against `fortress.AnyType.Any`; no team text ties Fortress `Object` to `java.lang.Object`. Java interoperability argues for `Any`, and the record never used an L3 ground for the bound. His hunch that layers were mixed is right in form; the crossing was L1→L2 on 09-20 (a WD sentence kept as the reason for a compiled-path setting), not L3→L1.
118	
119	**What he was told, and whether it changes the decision.** Told: that the compile path writes `Object` and this refuses tuples (true); that Steele switched the bound off in 2012 for the interpreter tests (true, half the story); that the Types chapter has `Object` exclude function types (wrong: it puts arrows under `Object`); that "nothing in the code changes because of it" (wrong: `Shell.java:372`). Not told: that Steele turned it on for the compiled path as a setting on 05-30; the code that reads the bound; the sentence's absence from 1.0. Had he been told all of it, the question under P-26 would have been "is Steele's 2012 setting the team's later word on the language?", and the answer above is no. His yes rested on the tuples; the tuples decide it. The decision stands and is stronger.
120	
121	**Where the entry misstates.** "Functions" (rq 218): the WD puts arrows outside `Object`, the Types chapter inside; drop the word, as the specification's callout already does. "The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure": the switch-over ends nothing by itself; `Shell.java:372` does, and no step named it (F-289, 685 errors under the command's setting).
122	
123	**Defaults.** P-42 stands (his; no change). The flip lands in 22c as one small rung: `Shell.java:372` to `false`, `XXXImplicitBoundAny` promoted, three pinned diagnostics rewritten, four `comprises` tests written `where [\E\]`, `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`'s premise rewritten with row 653 named, `CoercionGenericFnCompiledRungC` given `T extends Object` with a comment naming the prelude's `||` until the switch-over (the smallest edit that keeps the test's purpose; the other way is an `XXX` test). The probe's record actions: a ledger row for the tuple-domain dotted-method defect (section 12 of the ledger); row 339's "unverified" dropped; row 691's note; F-289 updated at the landing; the two FACTS the probe hands over. The flip is the coordinator's to schedule (P-42 promised it), named to him because he listed it among 22c's candidates.
124	
125	## 5. Phase 3's close: his framing is sound, and 22c carries four rungs
126	
127	- **Why the framing is sound.** J1024 §6 called phase 3 done by P-33's letter with its exit restated, and named a wider checker zero for phase 4. His framing moves the library-text and checker items that make the zero honest into one closing batch, so that phase 3 exits with a zero the switch-over can use: over the thirteen, under the compile command's own setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way. That is the first of J1024's two phase-4 zeros, brought forward; the code generator's zero stays phase 4's. It is the right cut: everything in 22c is checker or library text; everything left is code generation, run time or natives.

The two phase-4 zeros stand as J1024 named them.

136	- **Default:** yes, 22c with the four rungs; phase 3 closes at its gate; the four open words to him stay open (P-58's informed yes; the 40 components' place; rq 35; rq 230). Consequential; his (reads anew P-33's exit, which he framed).

138	## 6. Where this review's evidence changes an earlier ruling
139	
140	- **J1024 §2.3 item 2, §5.1 action 3, §5.2 item 8** placed P-42's flip "inside the names batch" with the compiled tests run once before. Changed: the flip lands in 22c, because the probe measured it at one small rung with the 27 `CompilerSystem` tests passing, because row 691 shows the command as it stands miscompiles, and because phase 3's zero must be measured under the command's own setting before the phase closes.

142	- **J0929 F3 and J1023 on P-26:** verdict unchanged; the limit named by the exclusion brief is now a rule in the entry (layer and date), and its "unfinished text" sentence is struck.
143	- **J1024 item 1 on row 816 / P-158:** verdict unchanged; the reason sharpened: an ambiguous L1 text read by the team's own checker, with the run-time death as the cost of the other reading, not "the compiled path's way wins" alone.
144	- **J0929 item 2's option 3 (`fail: Zilch`)** is now dated (Steele 2011-06-13) and ruled not binding; R0929 §1.8's instance rule stands as the fix.
145	- **The 09-20 library-route judgement §1** ("the compiler's setting is the spec's and the interpreter's is the divergence; the reconciliation keeps the compiler's") is overruled by P-42 and by this ruling: an L1 sentence of 2009 was read as the reason for an L2 setting, against the library's practice and the later texts.
146	- **J1023 V10 and R0929 §1.7 on P-42:** unchanged; two more L1 grounds (the WD's own instantiation sentence; the 2008 text's silence) and the L2 and L3 evidence are added.
