148	## 7. The POSITIONS rewrites: what each new text must make the coordinator do
149	
150	Scope: the writer drafts; the trap test checks. For each entry, the behaviour the text must produce in the coordinator at a fork, in plain words. Not the text.
151	
152	- **P-26.** Make the coordinator: (1) ask which layer a ground is in before weighing it, and never let a JVM or checker limit decide what the language says; (2) rank the team's language texts by date and by consistency, with the 2019 paper last; (3) count the team's code as the team's word on the language only where the team wrote the rule on purpose (a text, a commit message, a comment, or a checker rule enforced as the language's), and never a stub by the team's own words or an accommodation of a JVM or checker gap; (4) date a code commit against the texts before calling it "later"; (5) where two later sources conflict, stop ranking and decide by P-8's goal, saying so; (6) use one word for each of the two things called specialisation. Strike the "unfinished text" sentence. Trap: a 2009 prelude commit offered as "later" than a 2011 paper; a JVM `VerifyError` offered as a reason to change a specification sentence.
153	- **P-37.** Make the coordinator: (1) carry his reason of 10-26 (no port of walk's library into the compiler's; the checker continued until it accepts the fuller library); (2) know the switch-over has two gates, the checker's zero and the code generator's zero over the thirteen, and that no library jar has yet run compiled; (3) apply ruling 3's rule when a prelude shape differs from the library's; (4) treat the prelude as a bootstrap in L2 whose shapes are evidence, not authority. Trap: a prelude stub (fixed-arity `println`) offered against the library's varargs; a checker zero offered as proof the library runs compiled.
154	- **P-43.** Make the coordinator: (1) defend the flat numbers from the exclusion rule's four texts and the WD's "mutually exclusive" sentence, never from "the prelude did it"; (2) name the prelude's flat shape as the team's compiled-world instance of the same answer; (3) weigh any return to route C against F-46 and P-95, not against a speed sentence. The two sentences of rq 219 and 220 go to history. Trap: a worker proposes `ZZ32 extends ZZ64` because "the specification's library chapter says ℤ is a subtype of ℚ".
155	- **P-42.** Make the coordinator: (1) cite POPL 2019, the WD's instantiation sentence and the library's practice as the grounds; (2) say "tuples and `()`", not "functions"; (3) know the compiled path's `Object` is one line in `Shell.java` that 22c flips, not something the switch-over ends; (4) treat Steele's 2012 setting as the compiled path's enforcement of a WD sentence on one path, not the language's rule; (5) know that `()` as a static argument and the tuple-domain dotted method fail under either bound (rows 339 and new). Trap: a worker proposes keeping `Object` "because Steele set it in 2012" or "because Java's `Object` is the top".
156	- **P-33.** Make the coordinator: (1) read phase 3's exit as the thirteen under the compile command's setting, with operators and `abstract` read the team's way, closed by 22c; (2) carry two zeros into phase 4; (3) place the 40 other components before P-12's step or the first program that needs each, not before the switch-over; (4) know the code generator's half was unmeasured at approval and is 52 walls now. 157	- **P-7.** Make the coordinator read "later work in the compiler" through P-26's rule, not as a rule of its own; keep the baseline sentence. Trap: as P-26's.
158	- **P-12 and P-59.** Make the coordinator: (1) size P-12's step as three pieces (the Scala checker on under walk; walk reading `CoercionInvocation`; the imported components cleared) and call it unmeasured; (2) keep walk unchanged for static-type matters until then, as J1023 V3 applied it; (3) treat "microGPT's static types are concrete" as a premise to measure when microGPT compiles. Trap: a worker proposes `import java` in the library "because the specification has no `builtinPrimitive` rule".
161	- **P-158.** Make the coordinator cite the ambiguous text, the team's checker as the team's reading, and the run-time death as the cost of the other reading. Not a rewrite of substance; one sentence.
162	
163	## 8. Defects, decisions, questions
164	
165	- **Defects found by the inputs, to route:** the tuple-domain dotted-method death (new row, section 12); row 339 confirmed; row 691 reached through row 412; F-289 to update at the flip.
166	- **Decisions of mine in this judgement:** none in the tree; the rulings above, each with its default.
167	- **Decisions not taken, for later:** `CastError` checked against the prelude's unchecked `CastException`, once row 352's `throws` check is built; the tuple-rendering device (J1024 item 14), in the names batch.
168	- **Questions for him:** section 9's list.
169	
170	## 9. For Pavol
171	
172	**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.
173	
174	**The verdict, first.**
175	
176	- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
177	- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
178	- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.
179	
180	**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.
181	
182	- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
183	- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
184	- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
185	- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
186	- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.
187	
188	**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.
189	
190	- Both happened, and the sweep finds the choice was weighed every time the two differed on a design. Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
191	- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
192	- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.
193	
194	**The decisions to take, each with a default.**
195	
196	1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. The batch's exit: the checker reports no error over those thirteen parts, under the compile command's own setting. Everything that is about generating or running code stays in phase 4. Default: yes.
197	2. **Confirm that the 40 other library parts do not block the switch-over.** They hold 624 errors. They block the later step where the interpreter runs the checker on its own programs. Each is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it. Default: yes.
198	3. **Rewrite the reasons under five entries, through the trap test you approved.** The entries: the team's later word (P-26), one library (P-37), the flat numbers (P-43), the bound (P-42), the phases (P-33), and smaller corrections to five more. The new texts must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer and date "later" correctly. You said yes to this on 26 October. Default: proceed; nothing enters until a trap test passes.
199	4. **Three one-word answers, each in your own entry.** Drop "functions" from the bound's entry, since the team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. Default: drop. Strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" from P-26; the coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike. Move the two sentences of P-43's "Why" to history and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.
200	5. **Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23.** A native is a library function whose body is Java. The decision keeps the library's own form, `builtinPrimitive("...")`, and changes only the string, to name a static Java method both paths can call. The language has no rule here, so the library's practice decides. After the 449 bindings move, the other form costs a library sweep. Default: yes, as decided.
201	6. **One lean to confirm, no decision yet.** On 20 September you leaned to the class loader as the way to store a vector of doubles as a Java `double[]`. The lean was never recorded. Record it as a lean under the array decisions, to be measured; stamping a class per type, which the loader does today, gives no `double[]` field by itself. Default: record as a lean.
202	
203	**Two things to know, no decision needed.** The probe found a compiled-path defect that does not depend on the bound: a generic method with one tuple-typed parameter dies at the call. It gets a ledger row. And the small library's cast failure is an unchecked exception where the full library's is checked; this matters only when the checker starts checking `throws` clauses, and it will come to you then.

# The foundations of the revival: the judgement

## 0. How to read this

- **The three layers**, his frame of 2026-10-26 05:25 UTC. L1, the language: the Working Draft (WD, the team's text of 2010-12, copied 2011-02-02), the revised specification, the papers of 2011, 2012 and 2019, the 2012 restart's Types chapter, the team's library as a statement of the language, and the team's later published word. L2, the team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled path's checker, code generator, class loader and run time, the compiler's prelude, and walk. L3, Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer does not by itself decide a question in another. Where a team text in L1 itself argues from L2 or L3 (as the 2011 paper argues from Java), the text is the team's L1 word and its argument is theirs to make; I count it as L1.
- **Verdicts.** *Holds*: the tenet is right and its sound reason exists in the right layer. *Holds, text*: right, but its entry states a weaker, misplaced or wrong reason, or lacks the reason the coordinator needs to weigh a trade-off. *Bends*: against a team text where the team left a way the revival did not take. *Reverse*. None of the nine is a bend or a reversal.
- **Consequential** is the coordinator skill's test: reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; touches microGPT; chooses where the three principles split or are silent; or cannot be undone. A ruling so marked is his; each carries a default.
- **Earlier judgements**: J0929 (`decisions-review/judgement.md`), R0929 (`popl-recheck.md`), J1023 (`type-decisions-review/judgement.md`), J1024 (`phase3-exit/judgement.md`). I do not repeat their rulings; section 6 lists where this review's evidence changes one.

## 1. In short

1. **His doubt is answered: no foundational decision was a mistake.** All nine tenets hold. Three were taken on incomplete or partly wrong information (P-42, P-43, P-37), and in each case the missing or corrected fact makes the decision stronger or leaves it unchanged. None weakens it.
2. **The layers were mixed in the record's reasons, not in his decisions.** Four entries state a reason in the wrong layer or with the wrong date: P-26's list of "later word" counts 2009 prelude code as later than 2010-2012 texts; P-43's "Why" calls the prelude "the team's last record of the Fortress way"; P-37 lets the one library "take a design of the prelude's" with no rule for when; P-42 says "the switch-over ends the departure" where one line of `Shell.java` does. One judgement of 2026-09-20 read a WD sentence (L1) as the reason to keep a compiled-path setting (L2); P-42 corrected the language rule nine days later, and the code change is still owed. The rewrites fix the reasons; no decision turns.

## 3. The prelude question: when a design of the compiler's prelude binds the one library

**The coordinator's proposal:** when the team's later word on the language backs it, as the exclusion rule backs the flat number types; a bootstrap stub does not count.

**Ruling: right, with three sharpenings.**

1. **"Backs" is tested in L1 first.** A paper, the Types chapter, a specification sentence, a commit message or code comment that states the shape as the language's. The exclusion rule passes (four texts). The flat numbers pass through it and through the WD's "mutually exclusive".
2. **Where the L1 text is silent or ambiguous, the team's compiled checker enforcing the shape as a rule is the team's own reading of their text, and binds.** This is row 816's case: `apis.tex:252-256` reads as "no body needed" and is silent on the declaration; `source-code.tex:384-385` reads as the member declared either way; Chase's 2012 export checker counted every api member and refused a component that left one out. So P-158 holds, and its stated reason should be this, not "by P-26, the compiled path's way wins over the interpreter's library" alone.
3. **"Later" is a date, and a stub is a stub by the team's words.** A prelude line counts as the team's later word only if it is later than the library's text on the same shape and no later L1 text contradicts it. A line the team called "for now", "bogus", "bogo", "hack", "temporary", or that works around a checker gap (static arguments written at every generic call, fixed arities in place of varargs), is an accommodation and does not bind.

**Applied to the sweep.**

## 4. The bound: P-42 holds, on these grounds

**L1.** (a) POPL 2019, the type group's last published word, Steele and Ryu among the authors: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any" (`ParkPOPL2019.txt:418-419`). (b) The WD's `Object` sentence (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) is absent from the 2008 release (page 67), enters the repository in two bulk imports of 2009-11, the first in a chapter headed "Not Yet Implemented Features"; its composer is not recoverable. The same WD section says "Type parameters are instantiated with types such as trait types, tuple types, and arrow types" (`:53-54`), and the WD puts tuples, arrows and `()` outside `Object` (`types-vals-vars.tex:136`, `:215-216`); so under the WD's own `Object` default no unbounded parameter could take what the WD says parameters take. (c) The library, the team's statement of the language's library, declares its element parameters unbounded and instantiates them at tuples (`Generator[\E\]`, `zip`'s `(E,F)`); only six functions write `extends Any`. (d) The 2012 Types chapter states no default and makes `Any` the top with `Object` excluding `Void` and every tuple type (`types.tick:232-238`); Welterweight and the 2011 paper have `Any` as the top. (e) The team's own 2008 commit left the bound "(either Object or Any)" open. Naden's August 2012 theory calls `Object` "the distinguished top type" in a calculus with no tuples or arrows, where the two names coincide; it is not a vote for `Object` over tuples.

**L2, the archaeology's finding and how to read it.** Steele implemented the WD's sentence on 2012-05-28 ("amazingly, this was not yet implemented"), inserting `extends Any` into the compiled libraries and nine tests wherever they instantiated at `()`, a tuple, an arrow or `Any`; commented it out on 05-29 "so that interpreter tests will pass"; and on 05-30 made it a setting, on in `useCompilerLibraries`, off in `useInterpreterLibraries`. The brief's phrase "Steele's 2012 code chose `Object` as the language's rule" reads too much into it. His message says he was implementing a sentence already written, not deciding one; when the sentence broke walk's tests he did not change walk or the library, he confined the sentence to the compiled path; and he had to write `Any` by hand everywhere the compiled world needed tuples. No team text says the code generator, class loader or RTTI needs `Object` (archaeology §2.6, §5). The code reads the other way: Naden's dispatcher ignores a written `Any` bound as "meaningless" and checks any other (`OverloadSet.java:1516-1517`); `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` names an empty clause `Object` only in a generic method's name, which declaration and call compute alike. The team's texts after 2012-05-30 (Types, 05-31; Naden, 08-31; POPL 2019) do not carry `Object` as the default. So the setting is the compiled path's departure from the language's rule, L2, and ends by one line.

**L2, the probe.** Under `Any`, generic functions, objects, traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase` at a pair or an arrow compile, load and run, making the same classes and the same bytecode as with `extends Any` written; the 23 `CompilerSystem` `.test` files pass under both settings; `ant testQuick` under `Any` gives 12 failures in 10 compiler tests, all test-side (one promotion, three pinned texts, four `where [\E extends Object\]` workarounds of row 412, one premise, one prelude limit). Under `Object`, `q = id((3, 4))` compiles and runs `id(3)`, printing `q + 1 = 4` (row 691 reached by row 412): the compile command as it stands can silently miscompile. `()` dies under either bound (row 339, confirmed by `javap`); a generic dotted method with a single tuple-typed parameter dies under either bound (new, `CodeGen.java:6250-6263`, the team's comment "when generics can be parametrized by tuples"). Neither depends on the bound.

**L3.** `java.lang.Object` is translated to Fortress `Any` (`NamingCzar.java:447`); natives are written against `fortress.AnyType.Any`; no team text ties Fortress `Object` to `java.lang.Object`. Java interoperability argues for `Any`, and the record never used an L3 ground for the bound. ## 9. For Pavol

**What you asked.** On 26 October you wrote that you doubted whether the decisions the revival rests on were good and well informed, or a mistake. You named the bound as a possible linchpin, and you asked that the three layers be kept apart: what the Fortress language says; how the team built it on the Java virtual machine; and how Fortress meets Java.

**The verdict, first.**

- None of the nine foundational decisions was a mistake. All nine hold.
- Three of them were taken on information that was incomplete or partly wrong. In every case, the missing or corrected fact makes your decision stronger or leaves it as it is. None weakens it.
- The layers were mixed in the reasons written under your decisions, not in the decisions. Four entries give a reason from the wrong layer, or call a 2009 piece of code "later" than a 2011 paper. The rewrites fix the reasons. No decision turns.

**The bound, in plain words.** A type parameter is a placeholder for a type, like the `T` in `List[\T\]`. Its bound is the largest type the placeholder may stand for. `Any` is the type of every value. `Object` is the type of every value except tuples (pairs such as `(3, 4)`), functions, and the empty value `()`. You decided that a placeholder with no written bound means `Any`.

- The language, layer one, says `Any`. The team's last paper, from 2019, with Steele and Ryu among its authors, says in so many words that the default bound is `Any`. The team's library, which is their statement of the language's library, writes its placeholders without a bound and fills them with tuples. The 2011 draft's sentence saying `Object` is not in the 2008 text, appears in 2009 in a list of "Not Yet Implemented Features", and sits beside a sentence in the same section saying placeholders take tuple types, which `Object` would forbid.
- The team's build on the virtual machine, layer two, does not need `Object`. In May 2012 Steele implemented the draft's sentence on the compiled path, saying it was "amazingly" not yet implemented. The next day it broke the interpreter's tests. He did not change the interpreter or the library. He made the sentence a setting that is on for the compiled path and off for the interpreter, and he wrote `Any` by hand in every compiled library and test that needed tuples. That is enforcing a sentence on one path, not choosing the language's rule. No team text says the compiled path needs `Object`. A probe this week turned the setting off: tuples and functions as type arguments compile and run exactly as they do today when `Any` is written. With the setting on, as the compile command has it today, a call `id((3, 4))` compiles and silently runs `id(3)`.
- Java, layer three, maps its own `Object` type to Fortress `Any`, not to Fortress `Object`. Nothing in the record ever used Java as a reason for the bound.
- What you were told on 29 September had two errors: that "nothing in the code changes" (one line in `Shell.java` does), and that the 2012 Types chapter puts functions outside `Object` (it puts them inside; tuples stay outside). You were not told that Steele turned the setting on for the compiled path on purpose. Your yes rested on the tuples, and the tuples decide it. The decision stands.
- The bound is not a linchpin. Only one line of code and ten test files rest on it.

**The compiler's small library, in plain words.** The team built two libraries: the interpreter's full one, and a small one for the compiler that they called "bogus", a "bogo-trait" and a "hopefully temporary hack". You decided the full one is the one library, and you asked whether we ported the small library's good designs back or just taught the checker to accept whatever the full library said.

- Both happened, and the sweep finds the choice was weighed every time the two differed on a design. Taken from the small library: the flat number types, the numeral type, ranges over 32-bit integers, each integer type's own `MIN` and `MAX`, the integer power, lazy comparison, and the rule that a component declares every member its interface marks abstract. Weighed and not taken, with the reason now dated: the small library's `fail` returning a declared bottom type (Steele, June 2011), which the team's own 2012 and 2019 texts later made unwritable; the small library's `comprises T` spelling of the self type (Steele, June 2012), whose fact the checker now reads from the bound, as Naden's last note pointed; and string concatenation with the string on the left only, which the specification's own rule contradicts.
- The rule for the future, which goes into the record: a design of the small library binds the full one when the team's later word on the language backs it, or when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A stub by the team's own words does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper.
- One place we had the full library's text against a backed design of the small one: the abstract members (row 816). You reversed that on 25 October. The sweep finds no other.

**The decisions to take, each with a default.**

1. **Close phase 3 with climb batch 22c.** Phase 3 is the work that made the type checker accept the full library's twelve core parts without error. Your framing is sound. The batch carries four rungs: the abstract-member repair you decided; the nine operator headers that differ between interface and component, with the export check made to read operators; the two library parts that `List` imports and the count never checked; and the one line that gives the compile command the `Any` bound, with ten test edits. The batch's exit: the checker reports no error over those thirteen parts, under the compile command's own setting. Everything that is about generating or running code stays in phase 4. Default: yes.
2. **Confirm that the 40 other library parts do not block the switch-over.** They hold 624 errors. They block the later step where the interpreter runs the checker on its own programs. Each is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it. Default: yes.
3. **Rewrite the reasons under five entries, through the trap test you approved.** The entries: the team's later word (P-26), one library (P-37), the flat numbers (P-43), the bound (P-42), the phases (P-33), and smaller corrections to five more. The new texts must make the coordinator weigh in the right layer and date "later" correctly. You said yes to this on 26 October. Default: proceed; nothing enters until a trap test passes.
4. **Three one-word answers, each in your own entry.** Drop "functions" from the bound's entry, since the team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. Default: drop. Strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text" from P-26; the coordinator added it with no source. Default: strike. Move the two sentences of P-43's "Why" to history and write the language's grounds in their place. Default: yes.
5. **Say yes, informed, to the natives' form before batch 23.** A native is a library function whose body is Java. The decision keeps the library's own form, `builtinPrimitive("...")`, and changes only the string, to name a static Java method both paths can call. The language has no rule here, so the library's practice decides. After the 449 bindings move, the other form costs a library sweep. Default: yes, as decided.
6. **One lean to confirm, no decision yet.** On 20 September you leaned to the class loader as the way to store a vector of doubles as a Java `double[]`. The lean was never recorded. Record it as a lean under the array decisions, to be measured; stamping a class per type, which the loader does today, gives no `double[]` field by itself. Default: record as a lean.

**Two things to know, no decision needed.** The probe found a compiled-path defect that does not depend on the bound: a generic method with one tuple-typed parameter dies at the call. It gets a ledger row. And the small library's cast failure is an unchecked exception where the full library's is checked; this matters only when the checker starts checking `throws` clauses, and it will come to you then.

92:3. It follows the type group's latest word where the late texts split: Naden's construct "only in bounds", realised on the checker's own 2009 self type, with the 2012 calculus's refusal of a type variable in a clause left standing.

313:   - 2011-12-06, the compiler library has `Equality[\T\] comprises T` at its first reachable copy (`26718e298`, the ways note section 4).

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

{\it add}\ob{X <:{\tt Ring}\ob{X}}(X,X) : X~(*){\it def1}\\
{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

This forces us to recognize the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{\mathbb{Z}}$ as $\mathbb{Z}$ in order for {\it def1} to
apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

92:3. It follows the type group's latest word where the late texts split: Naden's construct "only in bounds", realised on the checker's own 2009 self type, with the 2012 calculus's refusal of a type variable in a clause left standing.

$\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

{\it add}\ob{Y <: {\tt Field}\ob{Y}}(Y,Y) : Y~(*){\it def2}\\
\end{array}$\\

apply which will automatically also mean that {\it def2} applies.  This approach suggests further that
the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot
be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds.  Victor and John have started working on this
sort of theory with their {\it trolls}.  However, the visibility problem shows that this is not sufficient to fix the
unsoundness problems with the cross instantiation.  Therefore, more work needs to be done in order
to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system.

<!-- The clarity workflow: rewrite POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own, with a cold read and a fidelity check, as a Workflow run; how to run it and what to do with its output. -->

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).
=====
<!-- The record test of 2026-10-13 kept as a kit to run again: ten scenarios over the entries of the record rule's trial, their key and rubric, the script that fills them from a copy of the repository, the reader's and the grader's briefs, and the blind grading of the first run. -->

# The record test, a kit

The test asks whether a worker or the coordinator decides as well from entries written to the record rule as from the old ones. The new texts are Parts 3 and 3b of `../record-rule-draft.md`, and the first run's result is its Part 4. Scenarios 9 and 10 test the pairs of Part 3b, an entry of POSITIONS with the FACTS entries that build it.

## The files

- `questions.md`: the ten scenarios. A `{FACTS n}` or `{POSITIONS n}` line stands for the entry numbered `F-n` or `P-n`, which was the entry on line n when the record was numbered.
- `key.md`: for each scenario, the right answer, the facts it rests on and where they live, the wrong answers, and the rubric (decision 0 to 2, sources 0 to 1). Its notes on scenarios 9 and 10 say what the duplication between FACTS and POSITIONS did. It is kept as the first run used it. `grades.md` § 5 lists seven slips that the grader found in it.
- `fill.py`: fills the questions from one copy.
- `brief-reader.md`: the reader's brief, with `@DIR@`, `@QUESTIONS@` and `@OUT@` to fill in.
- `brief-grader.md`: the grader's brief. It names the first run's scratch folder; put yours in its place.
- `grades.md`: the first run's blind grading. X is the new entries and Y the old.
- `grades-pilot.md`: the second run's grading, on the consolidation's pilot: one reader in the pilot's copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the old entries and Y the pilot's; 28 and 29 of 30.
- `grades-final.md`: the third run's grading, on the finished consolidation: one reader in its copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the finished record and Y the old entries; 30 and 28 of 30.
- `grades-scenario6.md`: scenario 6 run again on the final record (124.1K), its entry F-201 replaced by the `coordinator` skill's section that now holds it; graded by the coordinator, not blind: 3 of 3, as before.

## How to run it

1. Make two worktrees of `main` at one base, detached: `git worktree add --detach /home/user/record-test-p BASE`, and the same for `/home/user/record-test-q`. Copy p keeps the old entries; copy q gets the new ones.
2. In both copies, delete what would tell a reader about the test or show it the other copy's texts, and commit nothing: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, `HELD.md`, `process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md`, this folder, and their lines in `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`.
3. In copy q, put in the new texts. Replace each entry's line with its new text from Part 3, or from Part 3b where the entry is there too, as POSITIONS 48 and 60 are. Write each one with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py set` in the copy, which keeps the old line in the history file. Then run `record.py check --base HEAD` in the copy.
4. Check the placeholders. `questions.md` names each entry by its line number at `0f54a698b`, which is its number since the record was numbered. On another base, check that each number still names the entry that the scenario means (the titles in Parts 3 and 3b; a merged entry's number is gone), and change the number where it does not. `fill.py` checks only that the number names one entry.
5. Fill the questions, once for each copy, into a file outside both copies: `python3 fill.py /home/user/record-test-p questions.md OUT`.
6. Launch one fresh Opus reader in each copy, with `brief-reader.md`: `@DIR@` is the copy, `@QUESTIONS@` its filled questions, `@OUT@` its answers. The two briefs differ in nothing else. Each reader wrote about 0.4M tokens in the first run.
7. Blind the answers. Copy them to `grade/answers-X.md` and `grade/answers-Y.md` by a choice the grader does not see, and write which is which in a file that the grader is not given (`arms.txt` in the first run).
8. Launch one Fable grader with `brief-grader.md`. It reads `questions.md` unfilled, `key.md` and the two answer files, and checks against `main` any claim beyond the key. It wrote 0.75M tokens in the first run.
9. Unblind with the arms file, and report by "the new entries" and "the old entries", not X and Y.

To re-run one scenario after an entry is repaired, cut `questions.md` to that scenario, fill it from the copy, and give a fresh reader the same brief. Grade it against the same key. In the first run, the coordinator graded the re-run of scenario 7 itself, knowing its copy, so that grade was not blind.

3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

// the coordinator applies final.apply with record.py, files queue.md and commits. Nothing here touches the record.
const T = '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/'
const KIND = args.kind
const OUT = args.out
const cut = (s, n) => (s ? String(s).slice(0, n) : null)
const ASSESS = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: { rewrite: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } }, summary: { type: 'string' } },
  required: ['rewrite', 'summary'],
}
const STREAM = args.stream || args.chunks[0].name
const FROM = args.from || 'assess'

  const task = `Read your brief and follow it: ${T}${brief}. Your kind: ${KIND}. Your chunk: ${x.name}. Your entries: ${x.write.join(', ')}. Your folder: ${x.dir}`
  const log = `${x.dir}writer-${n}.log`, done = `${x.dir}writer-${n}.done`
  return agent(`You drive a long command and report its output; you judge nothing and write nothing else. The folder ${x.dir} may not exist yet: create it with mkdir -p.
1. If ${done} exists, skip to step 3.
2. Run this in the background with the Bash tool's run_in_background, exactly:
   ${T}writer-stream.sh ${STREAM} "${task}" > ${log} 2>&1; touch ${done}
3. Run \`python3 ${T}wait.py ${done} 540\` in the foreground, with a timeout of 600000 ms. If it exits 1, run it again; repeat until it exits 0.
4. Your final message: the last 60 lines of ${log}, verbatim.`, { label: `${n === 1 ? 'write' : 'fix'} ${x.name}`, phase: n === 1 ? 'Write' : 'Fix', model: 'sonnet' })
}
const tell = (x, extra) => `Your kind: ${KIND}. Your chunk: ${x.name}. Your entries: ${x.write.join(', ')}. Your folder: ${x.dir}` + (extra ? '\n' + extra : '')

const res = await pipeline(args.chunks,
  async (c) => {
    const dir = OUT + c.name + '/'
    if (FROM === 'judge') return { name: c.name, dir, write: c.entries, judgeOnly: true }
    if (KIND !== 'facts') return { name: c.name, dir, write: c.entries }
    const a = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}assess.md\n\nYour chunk: ${c.name}. Its entries: ${c.entries.join(', ')}. Your folder: ${dir}`,
      { label: `assess ${c.name}`, phase: 'Assess', model: 'opus', schema: ASSESS })
    return { name: c.name, dir, write: a ? a.rewrite : [], assess: a ? cut(a.summary, 1200) : 'assessment failed' }
  },
  async (x) => {
    if (!x.write.length) return { ...x, skipped: 'nothing to rewrite' }
    if (x.judgeOnly) return x
    const w = await drive(x, 1, 'writer.md')
    return { ...x, writer: cut(w, 1500) }
  },
  async (x) => {
    if (x.skipped || x.judgeOnly) return x
    const r = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}coldread.md\n\nThe file to read: ${x.dir}clean.txt\nYour report: ${x.dir}cold-read.md`,
      { label: `cold read ${x.name}`, phase: 'ColdRead', model: 'opus' })
    return { ...x, coldread: cut(r, 1000) }
  },
  async (x) => {
    if (x.skipped || x.judgeOnly) return x
    const r = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}check.md\n\n` + tell(x),
      { label: `check ${x.name}`, phase: 'Check', model: 'opus' })
    return { ...x, check: cut(r, 1500) }
  },
  async (x) => {
    if (x.skipped || x.judgeOnly) return x
    const r = await drive(x, 2, 'fix.md')
    return { ...x, fix: cut(r, 1500) }
  },
  async (x) => {
    if (x.skipped || x.judgeOnly) return x
    const r = await agent(`Read your brief and follow it: ${T}coldread.md\n\nThe file to read: ${x.dir}clean.txt\nYour report: ${x.dir}cold-read-2.md`,
      { label: `reread ${x.name}`, phase: 'Reread', model: 'opus' })
    return { ...x, reread: cut(r, 1000) }

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# writer-stream.sh STREAM TASK...: one task for a stream's headless Opus writer, resumed while its context
# is small and its prompt cache warm, started fresh otherwise.
#
# A stream is one writer that takes its chunks in turn, so that a chunk's fix round resumes the session that
# wrote it and holds its evidence in the cache: the clarity pilot's fix round wrote 61K tokens where a fresh
# writer reads everything again. A headless session keeps its cache for an hour; a Workflow agent's lives five
# minutes. The writer's standing brief is the skill writer's (../../skill-writer-brief.md), with the clarity
# writer's brief (writer.md, or the orientation's); TASK is the rest of the command line, sent as the task.
#
# A fresh session starts when the stream has none, when its context passes LIMIT tokens written (default
# 400K), or when its last task ended more than 50 minutes ago. Tasks of one stream run one at a time (flock).
# The state is under the repository's tmp/record-writer/STREAM/ (ignored): session, written, last, and each
# task's JSON. Prints the writer's report, then one line: session, new or resumed, tokens written.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)
stream=${1:?stream}; shift
task="$*"; [ -n "$task" ] || { echo "usage: $0 STREAM TASK..." >&2; exit 2; }
state="$repo/tmp/record-writer/$stream"; mkdir -p "$state"
LIMIT=${LIMIT:-400000}
tools=(Read Edit Write Glob Grep
       "Bash(python3 -I explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/entries.py:*)"
       "Bash(explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh:*)"
       "Bash(python3 explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py:*)"
       "Bash(git show:*)" "Bash(git log:*)" "Bash(git grep:*)" "Bash(git diff:*)" "Bash(wc:*)" "Bash(ls:*)")
cd "$repo"
exec 9>"$state/lock"; flock 9
now=$(date +%s)
fresh=1
if [ -f "$state/session" ] && [ -f "$state/last" ] && [ -f "$state/written" ]; then
  if [ $(( now - $(cat "$state/last") )) -lt 3000 ] && [ "$(cat "$state/written")" -lt "$LIMIT" ]; then fresh=0; fi
fi
out="$state/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).json"
if [ $fresh = 1 ]; then
  id=$(python3 -c 'import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())'); echo "$id" > "$state/session"; echo 0 > "$state/written"
  { cat explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md
    printf '\n# This session\n\nYou are a stream writer: the coordinating session sends you tasks one after another, each a chunk of record entries or a part of a skill to write or fix. Your standing order above holds for every task, except its parts on skill files, on committing and on sources.md, which your task brief replaces. Commit nothing.\n\n# Your first task\n\n%s\n' "$task"; } |
    claude -p --model opus --session-id "$id" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
      --allowedTools "${tools[@]}" --output-format json > "$out"
else

content.content:
1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
21	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
22	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
23	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
24	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
25	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
26	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
27	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
28	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
29	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
30	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
31	
32	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
33	
34	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
35	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
36	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
37	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
38	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. Run it on FACTS before each batch launches, since the batch's workers read it.

- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Three Workflow scripts make the record and the worker skill readable again when they drift. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Put the open questions of their runs on the review queue.

- The mining workflow finds where each POSITIONS entry came from: the curator's words, or an agent's summary or default. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- The clarity workflow rewrites POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is" (scope, present meaning, evidence, comprehension, ownership and consistency), and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Run it when entries no longer read on their own. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- The orientation workflow writes `fortress-repo`'s revival part, the short account of how revived Fortress differs from the original, which every worker reads whole. Its consolidate mode rewrites the whole part. Run it when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its update mode runs after each landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

Check each commit with `git show --stat`.
11. **The review queue:** one item for a decision not taken: the compiler prelude's cast failure (`CastException`) is unchecked and the one library's `CastError` is checked; the revival added about 50 casts; this needs a decision once the checker checks `throws` clauses (row 352). Your final message: each change (entry or row number, one line on what changed), the check commands' last lines, and anything you did not file and why.

<!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->

# What Pavol knows

A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.

- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.

## Topics

### Languages and tools

- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.

### Types and language design

- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".

### Mathematics

- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.

### Machine learning

- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.

### Fortress, its sources and the record

- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.

### Compilers and run times

- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

### The repository and the process

- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

## How to explain to him

- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

content.content:
- P-26 **Where the team's later word on the language conflicts with the specification's early text, the later word wins; each ground is weighed in its own layer, and "later" is a date.** The team's word has three layers. The language: the Working Draft of February 2011, whose text the team last edited in 2010-12, and `Specification/`, the revival's revision of it (P-7); the 2012 Types chapter; the type group's papers; and the team's library, the interpreter's, as their statement of the language's library. A team text of the language that argues from Java, as the 2011 paper does, still counts in the language. The team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled checker, the code generator, the class loader, the run time, the compiler's prelude and walk. Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer may confirm, but does not by itself decide, a question in another, and a JVM or checker limit never overrides what the language's texts say. Where those texts give no answer, the curator decides by the goal (P-8), and a ground in the implementation may weigh there (P-77). In the language, later texts that agree with each other rank above earlier ones, by year: the Working Draft (text of 2010), the type group's paper (2011, `Papers/Types/`), the Types chapter and Karl Naden's write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (both 2012, the write-up at `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`), and the POPL 2019 paper, the last (F-166). The team's implementation on the JVM: the compiled checker, the code generator, the class loader, the run time, the compiler's prelude and walk. Java interoperability: how Fortress types and natives meet Java's. A ground in one layer may confirm, but does not by itself decide, a question in another, and a JVM or checker limit never overrides what the language's texts say. Where those texts give no answer, the curator decides by the goal (P-8), and a ground in the implementation may weigh there (P-77). In the language, later texts that agree with each other rank above earlier ones, by year: the Working Draft (text of 2010), the type group's paper (2011, `Papers/Types/`), the Types chapter and Karl Naden's write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (both 2012, the write-up at `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`), and the POPL 2019 paper, the last (F-166). A stub by the team's own words, such as a line they called "bogus" or a "temporary hack", does not count, and neither does a workaround of a JVM or checker gap. Where two later sources conflict, this rule gives no order: the curator decides by the goal (P-8), and the record says that the goal decided it. Two things are called specialisation. A specialised overload is a version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time; it belongs to the language. Stamping is the class loader's making of one class for each instantiation; it belongs to the implementation. Why: the early text was a wish, written early and in a vacuum; the type group learned what is feasible by building it, with performance as the goal and specialised overloads a must; the revival knows less than they did and does not second-guess them. ## P-26

- P-26 **Where the team's later word on the language conflicts with the specification's early text, the later word wins; each ground is weighed in its own layer, and "later" is a date.** The team's word has three layers. The language: the Working Draft of February 2011, whose text the team last edited in 2010-12, and `Specification/`, the revival's revision of it (P-7); the 2012 Types chapter; the type group's papers; and the team's library, the interpreter's, as their statement of the language's library.
