<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.
- P-8 **Where the designers' own sources, the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations, give no answer, the curator decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and he stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** On the way to a compiled microGPT, he accepts the language's unfinished corners as they are, so that the work does not stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and he takes the designers to have known more than he does.
- P-9 **The revival searches for the most readable expression of the microGPT algorithm.** C4 is the flat microGPT program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), whose data layout follows Aaron Hsu's flat style of APL (P-29: C4 is not edited for speed before microGPT runs compiled). In C4, the polishing happens in the vocabulary, the array operations that the model's lines call: `FlatArrays.fss` beside C4, and what of it has moved into the standard library (P-27: what microGPT invented goes into the library). P-87 holds the limit: the model's text is the notation, and a change to a model line is shown to the curator as a diff first. C4 is the target form of the APL microGPT program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`): the APL program is written so that each of its lines expands into the line that C4 writes by hand. C4 writes its hyperparameters as tuple bindings, such as `(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)`, the form to which the APL sub-language (P-10) expands a strand assignment, APL's binding of several names at once. The one-line form, declarations separated by semicolons such as `nEmbd = 16; blockSize = 16; ...`, is not used: the APL sub-language has no use for it.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its sub-language covers only what the APL microGPT program needs, and the parts of APL that it left unbuilt, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, are not pursued.** The side quest built an APL sub-language in `explorations/apl/`: a DSL grammar that expands APL text into Fortress code over Fortress's native arrays, not an interpreter of APL. Its microGPT program, `explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`, stays in the microGPT check under walk (P-30: the check's limit of one minute; what the check runs: the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/interpreter.md`, "The model program").
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless the curator asks.** The 2D notation is Fortify's rendering. Fortify (`Fortify/`, run by `bin/fortify` and `bin/fortick`) typesets Fortress source as mathematics in LaTeX, for the specification and the papers. Taken as programming syntax, such a rendering fixes one view of a computation, though the same mathematics can be written in many ways. APL, with one symbol for each transformation of the data, expresses a computation better. The rendering is presentation only, off the revival's path, and no argument in favour of Fortress. The verdict is on that typesetting only: the Unicode operators, such as `∑` and `×`, are the language's own syntax.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-19 **The tree is not described as the third-party port's migration grafted onto the team's history.** The port is a third-party port of the tree to Java 9, which commit `8fe1daa8f` copied onto the team's last commit (the `fortress-repo` skill, `references/records.md`, "The repository's history"). By history, `main` descends from that commit. By content, most of the port's files are removed or redone, and only one piece of the port's code still runs: the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash (F-165). Why: the tree is not built on the port, and the record must not lead anyone to think that it is. The files that still describe the tree so wait for the lineage cleanup; `coordinator/lineage.md`, "Files that still repeat it", lists them.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it (P-26: the specification is revised to the team's later word). Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper (F-166). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
- P-28 **Fleshing out the standard library is a very important task.** Its next layer is algebra: traits such as `Ring` and `Field`, which the library does not declare yet, and what machine learning's matrices and tensors need, so that the library's algebraic traits, such as `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`, reach them too. Why: the curator wants those matrices and tensors to have the mathematical rigour that the library's way of building its types promises. The work edits the standard library itself, in `Library/`, not a separate tree of the revival's own outside it (P-27, how the library is extended). It is parked off the path to microGPT compiled. Two matrix ideas of his wait beside it: square matrices of one size as a multiplicative ring, and diagonal matrices of one size as a ring whose product commutes.
- P-29 **Walk's speed is irrelevant to every judgement of Fortress's performance.** Walk is far slower than Python's interpreter (`explorations/microgpt-port.md`, "Step-0 results", a measurement of 2026-08-23). Fortress's performance is judged on the compiled path, once the compiler runs programs. So no performance decision rests on walk's timings. In particular, until microGPT runs compiled, C4, the flat microGPT program, is not edited for speed. The gate never runs microGPT's two programs, C4 and the APL-style program, because they run too long to be tests. Why: walk is the unoptimised path, as a debug build is in Swift, where performance is not judged either.
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.
- P-32 **The record's maps are kept current and used, so that nothing that the record holds is worked out again from scratch.** The maps are `FACTS.md`, `INDEX.md` and the territory map, `explorations/coordinator/map/`. The territory map surveys the repository down to where the team wrote the intent of each design. Part of that intent is written only in the papers under `Papers/`, not in the specification. So the map covers the papers too, and shows where to look up a design's intent. `INDEX.md` is read whole at the coordinator's boot, at the start of each session and after each compaction, and each worker's brief carries a mission briefing from the territory map, not the whole map. The territory map's surveys date from 2026-09-16 (its README), so a status or a line number in them can be stale.
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3, the compiled checker reports no error on the interpreter's whole library (the distance to the switch-over at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value); phase 4, the switch-over, first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled). The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library. The decision is not put to him again. How the checker comes to accept the library, its first step and the order of the work, was left to a plan for him, which he approved (P-33).
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's defects are not repaired: they go with it at the switch-over.** Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.
- P-39 **Every batch's gate measures the checker count, and its total never turns the gate red.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. Its gate runs the gate's steps on their merged tree, and then the checker count, as step 8 (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`); the gate of `fortress-repo`'s gate part has no such step. The checker count and the distance to the switch-over both count the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library. The count stops where the checker crashes or meets an error that it cannot get past; the distance counts every error, over all apis and components (F-53 defines both and holds their values). A rise of the count's total is reported and never fails a batch on its own. The count's stage can still turn the gate red on the faults that F-66 names. One is a checker crash that no rung of the batch listed in advance as expected, in the field `expectedCheckerCrash` of the batch's manifest, the part of the batch's script that declares each rung's task. The gates of batches whose work drives the distance down also measure the distance, in a stage that only reports. Why: the distance's full measurement takes far longer than the count, and a batch pays for it only when the distance is the number that it tries to move.
- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array dies with a raw Java exception (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
- P-41 **On the compiled path, a size static argument travels at run time as a descriptor object, as a type argument does.** A generic type's descriptor has a field for each of its static parameters that is not an operator. The team's code generator already emitted that field for a size, with nothing to put in it, and the size's descriptor fills it. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor, which `RTTIsize.of` takes from a table; no Java class is written for it. This is the team's pattern for instantiating types, applied to numbers. An operator static argument, by contrast, stays a name known only at compile time (F-39, how both paths carry it). The curator sees no need for an operator argument to be carried at run time the way types and sizes are. F-129 holds what runs and its open rows.
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`, and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412).
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, whose `where` form is not built. `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25, P-26), and by them the clause is right as written. - P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar-extension block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** The vocabulary, the array operations that microGPT is written in, declares none of these six operators, an array with a number on either side; the library's scalar-extension block, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, serves them. `Diag`, the vocabulary's diagonal matrix, extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, the method that the library's matrix product calls, so `diag(v) m` scales the rows of `m` without forming the matrix. This is what the type system promises: a diagonal is a kind of matrix, with a faster product of its own. Row 299 records what the general product costs on a diagonal: 13 to 54 times as much as scaling the rows. Since the diagonal is read-only, a read-only matrix trait, `ReadableArray2`, which `Array2` would extend as `Array1` extends `ReadableArray1`, is also wanted (row 798): it is a library change, not a definition in the vocabulary.
- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function.** On the library's arrays, `fill(v)` fills an array with the value `v`, even when `v` is a function, and `tabulate(f)` fills it with `f` applied to each index. The function form, formerly an overload of `fill`, takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Why: in every peer language that has `fill`, `fill` takes the value.
- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked.
- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** An object with no `asString` of its own prints its Fortress type name as walk spells it, such as `Box`, or `Box[\ZZ32\]` for an instance of a generic object, with no marker and no hash code. A debug marker, such as the Java class name that the curator first leaned to, belongs in `asDebugString` if one is still wanted, not in the printed form; walk's `asDebugString` prints `a Box: Box`. Row 363: an `asDebugString` that prints as walk's does, where the compiled one prints `Box`. Row 321: printing an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument member named `toString`, which overflows the stack. Once the compiled path reads the one library, every object inherits such a member, the `getter toString` of that library's `trait Object`, so every object with no `asString` meets the overflow.

### The specification's revision

- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** When the revival changes the language, it updates `Specification/` with the change, so that the text and the implementation do not disagree. The original text and the reasoning are kept, so that route C stays open. Route C is the design that P-43 set aside: a nested number tower, under the forest rule of the team's 2012 patent applications (F-46 gives what a return to it would need). Every such change takes the revision form (P-96 gives its parts). The unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, is never touched. Why: an open disagreement between the text and the implementation would confuse a reader.
- P-96 **A change of the specification is shown in layers, as the team showed its own changes in the 1.0 release of 2008 and in the working draft of 2009.** This form is the revision form. A callout that prints in every build marks each changed passage; a `\note` will not do, since a release build hides it. Appendix I's revival section has an entry for each change: its reason, its original text, what a return to route C would mean for it, or that it would be the same under route C (P-95 says what route C is), and the decision that it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a document in the repository holds the full reasoning. Citations call the unrevised copy, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, the Working Draft of February 2011: the copy is that draft byte for byte, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 release (F-163). The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` gives each part in full, including what else an Appendix I entry holds.
- P-97 **The specification's examples that break the exclusion rule take the library's shapes, and each original stays, marked "Not allowed".** The Working Draft offered such examples as legal. Each now shows the shape that the library uses for the same thing, with the original beside it under the specification's own mark, "Not allowed". The specification states the rule, which it calls instantiation exclusion, once, in the two parts of Luchangco's Types chapter of 2012 (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`; P-25): `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` says which instantiations exclude each other, and `basic/traits.tex` says that a declaration may not extend two that do. The covariance example, a trait that extends other instantiations of itself, is rewritten and marked in the same way. Its callout adds one sentence: the type group's later design, in the same Types chapter, declares variance with a `covariant` modifier, which neither walk nor the compiled path implements (row 404 records the gap). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules as the team wrote them, under a callout that they predate the rule.
- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that the library's `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` work over total comparisons.** It does so in the library's api and component, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss`. It keeps the five members that it restates by hand: `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `<=` and `>=`. Without the parent, walk finds no overload of `BIG MIN` or `BIG MAX` that takes total comparisons (row 461). Why: it is the library's own device, which its other ordered types use. The curator took it on the coordinator's recommendation. It stands and blocks no work.

### The suites and the gate

- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every edit of source code in the original tree starts from a failing test. The worker adds the test to the test suite, sees it fail, makes the fix, and sees it pass. The test then stays in the suite for good. An edit of the specification or of documentation is not source code and needs no test. The gate's three test runs, `ant testFast`, `ant testSystem` and `ant testSpecData` (P-124), must pass when the work lands; they need not pass after every edit. The test and the fix may land in one commit. Why: the rule replaces one-off validation scripts, which no later build runs. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/tests-writing.md` says how to write the test.
- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test's result is pass or fail, as the team designed the suites. A value that matters is checked inside the test, with the checks that the harness already has: an `assert` call in an interpreter test, a `run_out_equals` key in a compiled test's `.test` file. What a test prints beyond its checks does not count. So no expected-output files are added. They are not proposed to the curator again, and neither is a comparison of what a test prints beyond its checks with an earlier run's output. Why: when the suite's designers let a test pass without a further check, what it prints need not be checked.
- P-124 **The specification's examples are a step of the gate, and every one must pass.** `ant testSpecData` runs the examples extracted from `Specification/` under walk (F-114 says which 130 it runs), and the gate fails if any of them fails. When an example fails, the implementation is fixed: the example is not respelled to get around a gap in walk, and no list of examples allowed to fail is kept.
- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** `build.xml` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS` to 4 for the two suites, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`, so that every run of them uses four threads, whatever the calling shell sets. A test that parallelism makes fail, on every run or only on some, is written wrong, for example a write that needs `atomic`, or it shows a defect. Either is fixed, never hidden by running at one thread. Why: Fortress is parallel by default, so a suite at one thread has a blind spot, and sparing the four-CPU machine is no reason for one.
- P-150 **No resident compiler is built.** A background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did, would save too little of the workers' time to be worth building (F-234), so the speed work goes to the checker itself (P-148). It is not tried again unless something significant changes.

All times UTC; his time was UTC+2 until 01:00 UTC on 10-25 and UTC+1 after. His messages are quoted in the session transcript `fe616d40-…jsonl` at the times given. This file holds what was understood and agreed; POSITIONS holds only what he decided, and the boot note what is in flight.

## 3. Row 816 and P-158 (10-25 19:06 to 10-26 04:28)

**The argument, in the order he asked for it (19:35:13):**

1. *The two paths call a method differently.* Walk finds a method on the object by name at the call; the trait need not declare it. The compiled path calls through the trait's Java interface; if the trait does not declare the method, the call dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). The team's export check enforced it (its count written by Sukyoung Ryu, `ac0d41de0`, 2009-05-08; first written here as Chase's of 2012, `5a68404fd`, a parentless snapshot): a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, the team's check refused 12 such members. Two ways: (a) add the 12 declarations to the components, the compiled library's way; (b) weaken the check. Climb batch 21b's rung E took (b) (`031c38bbc`), from a misreading of `apis.tex` ("includes definitions for all declarations other than … abstract" read as "needs no member", where it says "needs no body"). The chain: an Opus ways worker of 10-20 (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, "4i", "Decision: none, since it is the text's own rule"); the export probe of 10-23 built it; batch 21's planner made it fork 20 with the default "the team's own text"; its Fable review and I passed it as not consequential; rung E built it; its skeptic found the `NoSuchMethodError` after the build; the 21b review kept it as "it cannot happen yet"; batch 22 carried it as question 1 and I launched batch 22 at about 02:01 on 10-24 without sending him the question. Root cause: one sentence misread; nobody read the code it changed (the team's deliberate count) or asked what a compiled call does; the change cleared errors, which was the batch's goal.

No body, not an empty body: an empty body makes the method concrete, and then no object must define it.

**His decision:** option 2 (19:06:08 on 10-25); his reason (04:28:41 on 10-26): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." <!-- What Pavol, the curator, knows, graded by topic, for pitching an explanation or an ask at him, with each line's evidence in PROFILE-sources.md beside it. -->

# What Pavol knows

A topic reads `topic — level — how to pitch it`. `1 → 3` is a level that rose: pitch at the later one.

- 4, expert: hands-on depth; talk as to a peer.
- 3, working: uses it correctly; no explanation, define only the project's own terms.
- 2, familiar: knows the idea, not the details; a one-line reminder before it is used.
- 1, heard of: knows the name; explain it with one concrete case before using it.
- 0, new: explain from the ground up, concrete cases first, with the shortest grounding that worked where there is one.

## Topics

### Languages and tools

- Benchmarking and measurement statistics — 4 — talk as to a peer; frame speed results this way.
- Swift as a library and benchmark writer — 3 — his first frame; its compiler's insides, and its names for unique references and copy-on-write, are 1.
- Scala (2.8 era), Java and the JVM, Python, iOS, as a user — 3 — take as known; their compilers' insides are new.
- Rust, Julia, Kotlin, Clojure, C++ templates — 2 — one line on the peer's idea; Clojure's multimethods are 1.
- What generators cost against a loop — 3 — he measured it himself; use it for big operators.
- APL — 0 — the side quest is closed.

### Types and language design

- Type theory, formally — 0 — a concrete Fortress program and several cases before any rule.
- Dispatch on all arguments; exclusions; coercion against subtyping; `Any` against `Object` — 1 → 3 — take as known.
- The checker's overload rules — 1 — the idea stuck, the rules didn't; show concrete pairs of declarations.
- Erased against kept generics; traits that give behavior; a subtype with its own operation — 3 — he judges by ergonomics and reuse, not purity.
- `where` clauses; soundness — 0 → 2 — remind him that `where` narrows where a declaration applies.
- `nat` size parameters — 0 → 2 — remind him that a `nat` is a size the type carries; arithmetic on sizes is 0.
- An interface against a trait — 1 — he is unsure of the words; say "extends".

### Mathematics

- Matrix and vector products, the dot product — 1 — he knows only that inner dimensions match; start from a 2×2 matrix times a vector, show that order matters, then C4's shapes: 16×16 (attention), 27×16 (token table), 64×16 (feed-forward).
- Rings, fields, additive groups — 0 — no grounding has worked yet.
- Identity elements on each type's algebra — 3 — take as known.
- Q, Z and N; `ZZ` signed, `NN` not — 0 → 3 — take as known.
- The library's number types — 2 — bottom up, `ZZ32` first; top down failed.
- Floating point — 2 — he knows IEEE rounding against Java's; infinities among the rationals were new.
- Reshape, ravel, outer product, tensor — 0 — define each on a small array.
- Mathematical notation — 1 — set it beside the Fortress code that computes it.

### Machine learning

- micrograd, microGPT, nanoGPT; FP32; integer tokens — 3 — take as known; microGPT's baseline is CPython or NumPy.
- KV cache, loss curves, early stopping, Chinchilla — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- Backpropagation, functional or tape-style, and its cost — 1 — his views are guesses.
- Big operators as ML papers write them — 1 — "hardly a yardstick", he says.
- Attention and softmax — 0 — learning them was microGPT's point for him; teach from C4's code.

### Fortress, its sources and the record

- Steele's talks: juxtaposition, undefined precedence, parallel loops, inference, units, `Σ` over new types — 3 — take as known.
- Where intent lives: the papers, the TeX not the PDF, the team's later word, the library among the sources — 3 — his rules.
- Who did what: Ryu's front end, Park's POPL 2019 paper — 3 — take as known.
- The library's shape: `Vector` and `Matrix` for numbers only — 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The specification, the papers, the library's text — 1 — unread; quote the line that decides.
- Reading Fortress code — 1 → 2 — he reads a declaration line by line; gloss each new construct.
- `label` and `exit`, `comprises`, `atomic`, `thrower`, `reflect`, DSL blocks, where whitespace counts — 0 — one concrete case each.
- FACTS, POSITIONS, the original protocol — 0 — never read; say what an entry says.
- Walk against the compiled path; the compiler's prelude — 0 → 3 — take as known.

### Compilers and run times

- JVM performance: boxing, the JIT, specialization, unboxed doubles — 1 → 3 — where he grew most.
- The pipeline, the caches, JVM array limits, warm-up, races hidden by one thread — 3 — take as known.
- Loom, the Vector API, Truffle, GraalVM — 0 → 2 — a one-line reminder.
- The class loader and its descriptors — 0 → 2 — from his own picture: sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names, so the JIT drops bounds checks.
- One-time facts: which phases run the checker, the earlier compiler, a coercion's cost at run time, a load of 30 — 1 — one line when it comes up.
- The checker count and the distance to the switch-over — 1 — each time: what each counts, and why one can jump.

### The repository and the process

- Git; Claude Code's client; test-first, with `XXX` tests until a fix flips them — 3 — take as known.
- The platform: remote sessions, secrets in a container, the weekly reset — 1 — one line when it matters.
- The project's own terms; his past rulings — 2 — he forgets them after a gap; restate them by content.
- POSITIONS, "History he knows", and his decisions — 3 — take as known; cite a decision by what it says, never by its number.
- The coordinator's three principles — 1 — he knows the nine-step form, not these.

## How to explain to him

- Pitch at a software engineer who directs the work, not a researcher. Say what a feature costs.
- Concrete cases before the rule: several, on C4 or a Fortress program. He checks them for a contradiction, then takes the rule.
- Frame in what he knows, his own analogies first: the complex-number Mandelbrot, the diagonal matrix, Swift's debug builds, LLVM's lit.
- Define each term where it is used.
- Show Fortress code as Fortress, infix, not calls. Set notation beside the code. Draw a picture where structure matters.
- An ask: the question, context with a primer, numbered options with trade-offs and none that does nothing, the ask, the recommendation last. On types: the specification and the team's later word first, then the library, then the peers as context only. Say what each option does for a fast microGPT.
- One ask at a time, answerable as "3b". Show the wording before a yes. Mark a decision surfaced for his learning as one.
- Length by mode: three lines and "holding" while he reads turn by turn; an ask 1.5K to 3.3K, 5K with a refresher; long only to establish facts, never unasked.
- If he answers a long turn piece by piece: hold, list his points, and wait.
- When he's tired: one item, a default he can take, an offer to come back to it.
- When he ends "how wrong am I?": answer it, and reflect his idea back refined.
- He reads fast and forgets: restate, don't refer back.
- Plain words, halfway to ASD-STE100, positive phrasing.
- The phone, with Speak: a Select button per section, links not paths, no tables, numbers as K and M. A stop can be an accidental tap.
- Dictation: repair a term silently unless two readings differ. Seen, as heard → meant: forty five → Fortify, contact → compact, WordPress → Fortress, Table → Fable, scalar → Scala, Perl → parallel, Docker → checker, time system → type system, rank → rung, net → nat, Sue → Hsu, Popple → POPL, 16 → 64.

## Words to avoid

- A bare label: "P1", "row 40", "answer 9", "the judge", "the line". Name the thing.
- "Closure" for the integer tower; "sealed" for `Σ`; "revising the specification" for reconciling its contradictions.
- "Tensor", "reshape", "ravel", "outer product", "ring", "field", undefined; "coercion" for "conversion".
- "Yesterday"; "we" for him and Claude; a coda, a slogan, a clever turn.

## Open contradictions

- Length: he demands short replies, yet praised a long one while facts were being established.
- Reading: he says he hasn't read the specification or the library, yet spot-checks them and recalls Steele's talks exactly.
- Type theory: he says he knows none, yet reasons soundly about coercion, bounds and erasure.
- Scala: he says it earned his Stack Overflow points; most of the account is iOS.
- Peers: he asks what they do, yet rules that they only decide between the designers' choices; "context only" is the record's reading.
- Ownership: he wants every choice, yet at times takes a default unread.
- History: he recalls `main` as free of the third-party port; the record says otherwise.
- Other languages: his claims about them are unchecked; check one before building on it.

content.content:
1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. 2

4	
5	**writer**
6	: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.
7

9	: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.
10	
11	## The method
12	
13	1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
14	2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
15	3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
16	4. Publish the part as a page. The curator reads it whole.
17	5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
18	6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. Ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter.
19	
20	- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
21	- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, and keep the review page in step.
22	- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
23	- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
24	- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
25	- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
26	- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 3). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.
27	
28	## The coordinator skill
29	
30	This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:
31	
32	- Guide lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to the curator in each situation. Write no set of many small rules that may contradict each other.
33	- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
34	- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
35	- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
36	- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.

2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. Publish the part as a page. The curator reads it whole.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. Ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, and keep the review page in step.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 3). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- Guide lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to the curator in each situation. Write no set of many small rules that may contradict each other.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.

You are a retrieval worker for the Fortress revival repository at /home/user/fortress. Your task is an inventory: find each piece of work that was produced in one stretch of the project, and describe each one briefly. You describe; you do not judge which pieces are good or which to keep.

## The problem

From 06:11:21 UTC on 2026-10-26, the coordinating session ran a review of the project's foundational positions (the "foundations review"): scouts and probes gathered evidence, a Fable judgement weighed it, and the review found points on about 13 entries of `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md` that may each call for a small correction. A clarity workflow then rewrote those 13 entries, a trap test checked the new texts, and a page showed them to the curator. The curator rejected the 13 texts. He wants the evidence and the reasoning kept where they are sound, so that small, targeted corrections can be written from them. From now on, record text is written by Opus only; Fable may only comment on text that Opus wrote. So for each piece we need to know who wrote it and what it holds.

The curator's words: "let the worker do an inventory of artifacts produced, characterize them briefly, and then we'll devise a plan how to combine it into something good."

## The window

From 06:11:21 UTC on 2026-10-26 to now. In the session transcript, find the curator's message that contains the words "well aligned", and mark each piece as made before or after that message.

- Git, on `main`: `git log --since='2026-10-26T06:00Z' --name-status` for files under `explorations/`. Bound the output.
- The session transcript: `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.jsonl`. It is very large: search it with `grep` or a short Python script, never print it whole. Each assistant line carries a `model` field.
- The Agent-tool workers: `/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/subagents/agent-*.jsonl`. The first user message is the worker's brief; the assistant lines give its model.

Find which model each role of a run used, from the run's script (its `model` options) or from the agents' transcripts.
- A starting list: the curator asked at 05:22 UTC on 2026-10-27 "List the artifacts and reports produced after I said: Now we are well aligned". The coordinator's reply after that message in the transcript is a list to check against git. It may be incomplete.
- `explorations/conversations/02-phase3-exit-foundations.md`, sections 5, 8 and 9, and `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md` name many of the pieces and the pages' URLs.

## For each piece

- its path or page URL, and its commits;
- its size, in K characters;
- who wrote it: the coordinating session or a worker, and the tier (Opus, Fable or Sonnet), with how you know;
- what it holds, in at most three plain sentences;
- whether it names points on given POSITIONS entries: which entries, by number, and whether the points are evidence and reasons, or proposed wording for an entry;
- whether it was published as a page, and whether it is pushed to `origin/main`.

## Rules

- Read the headings and the opening section of a long report; grep it for `P-` numbers. Do not read long reports whole.
- Bound every command's output.
- Change nothing in the tree except your one output file. Run no build, test or workflow.

## Output

Write `explorations/reviews/foundations/evidence/salvage-inventory.md`. Start it with an HTML comment of one sentence that says what the file is. Group the pieces: 1, the review's evidence (scouts, probes, sweeps); 2, the judgement; 3, the rewrite, with the workflow's outputs by role; 4, the trap test and its results; 5, the pages; 6, other work in the window, such as climb batch 22c's planning, one line each. Then add a list by entry: for each POSITIONS entry that any piece names a point on, the entry's number and the pieces that hold such points. Keep the file under 12K characters. Write plain short sentences, without shorthand.

The write of the file may be refused. So end your final message with the file's full text.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

content.content:
<!-- The clarity workflow: rewrite POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own, with a cold read and a fidelity check, as a Workflow run; how to run it and what to do with its output. -->

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).
======
<!-- The clarity workflow's writer brief: rewrite record entries (POSITIONS or FACTS) so that a reader who knows the language but never saw the work behind them understands each one; meaning unchanged. From the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (positions-audit/clarity/). -->

You are the writer of the clarity pass in the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. First read your standing brief, `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`, sections 1 to 4, and follow them: the register and the writing principles. Its parts on skill files, on being a resumed session and on committing do not apply here: you write record entries, and you commit nothing.

Your launch message gives your kind (`positions` or `facts`), your entries and your folder. Change no tracked file but the files in your folder.

## The problem

The record is the project's memory, under `explorations/coordinator/`. `POSITIONS.md` holds the curator's decisions; the curator is the person in charge of the project. `FACTS.md` holds what is established about the tree. Their entries are too compressed: they lean on handles, short forms and phrasing that make sense only to someone who was in the conversation or the batch that produced them. Rewrite your entries so that a reader who knows the language, or can look its terms up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell without that history:

- for a position: what the curator decided, where it applies and its limits, what it requires a worker to do, and what is unfinished;
- for a fact: what is established and under which conditions (path, library, call form, values), what it means for the work and its limits, and its evidence.

Keep the meaning.

## Read first

- The standard: `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`. For positions, its sections "P45: fidelity and comprehensibility are separate checks" and "For Fable: rewrite positions before consolidating Revival". For facts, "For Claude: assess all FACTS, rewrite only failing entries", its entry schema above all.
- What an entry holds: `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`, "What an entry is".
- Your entries and their evidence:
  - positions: `python3 -I explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/entries.py N...` prints each entry and the provenance audit's evidence: the scout's report on the curator's messages behind it, with his exact quotes, and the audit's judgement, corrections and takeaway sections. Read the evidence before you write an entry.
  - facts: `assessment.md` in your folder holds the assessor's table and, for each entry you are given, what fails and why. `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'F-N+'` prints an entry with its linked entries, and `'history:F-N'` its history. Read the report section each entry cites before you change a claim.

## How to write each entry

1. The bold title states the decision or the fact in plain words, no broader than the body.
2. Then its scope and its exact conditions. Keep every condition, exception and limit. A shorter sentence must not lose one.
3. For a position, the reason after "Why:", only if the curator gave one or accepted it in the question. For a fact, its evidence: the test, measurement, source reading or report section, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred.
4. Keep the state apart: "Built.", or "Still to build:" in one line with where the work is tracked. Keep such lines as they are; do not move them out.
5. Name each thing. Say which call, which checker, which library, which path, when a sentence has two of them. Use no handle of a past conversation or batch ("answer 9", "ask 3", "item 48", "rung C", "decision E") unless a skill defines it.
6. **Pointers.** For each pointer (another entry, a gap-ledger row, a PLAN item, a report), decide first whether it belongs in the entry. If it stays, give it a few words on what it holds, so that a reader can decide whether to follow it without loading it. If it is only provenance, move it to the apply file's note line, where a bare reference is fine.
7. **Concepts.** Define a concept in the entry only if it belongs to this entry alone. List any other concept that a reader needs in `concepts.md` in your folder: the term, the entries that use it, and where it should be defined for every worker (the `fortress-repo` core, an area part, or the short orientation that will replace the revival part). The revival part is being rewritten: do not lean on it.
8. Do not add a claim, a reason or a scope that the sources do not hold. Do not make a claim stronger or broader. Where the sources leave the meaning open, keep the current wording for that part and write a question for the curator.
9. For a fact: keep a historical measurement only if it is stated as that measurement; move repair chronology to the history; link a count that changes at every landing to the entry that owns it. A fact may record an implementation choice made at a default; say so, and never as the curator's ruling.
10. Keep each entry near 600 characters as a check, not a cap. Clarity comes first.

## Your files, in your folder

- `proposals.md`, with a header comment of one sentence. For each entry: the clean entry first, as the record would hold it; then "Meaning: unchanged", or each change of meaning you could not avoid, with its source; then the source of each sentence; then any question for the curator.
- `clean.txt`: the clean entries only, one per line. A cold reader gets this file alone.
- `proposals.apply`: each entry's line, then one indented line `  by: the clarity pass; note: WHY`, with the provenance pointers that left the entry. The coordinator applies it with `record.py`.
- `concepts.md`, as in step 7.

Your final message: the files' paths, and one line per entry on what made it hard to read and what you did.
======

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

The test asks whether a worker or the coordinator decides as well from entries written to the record rule as from the old ones. The new texts are Parts 3 and 3b of `../record-rule-draft.md`, and the first run's result is its Part 4. Scenarios 9 and 10 test the pairs of Part 3b, an entry of POSITIONS with the FACTS entries that build it.

## The files

- `questions.md`: the ten scenarios. A `{FACTS n}` or `{POSITIONS n}` line stands for the entry numbered `F-n` or `P-n`, which was the entry on line n when the record was numbered.
- `key.md`: for each scenario, the right answer, the facts it rests on and where they live, the wrong answers, and the rubric (decision 0 to 2, sources 0 to 1). Its notes on scenarios 9 and 10 say what the duplication between FACTS and POSITIONS did. It is kept as the first run used it. `grades.md` § 5 lists seven slips that the grader found in it.
- `fill.py`: fills the questions from one copy.
- `brief-reader.md`: the reader's brief, with `@DIR@`, `@QUESTIONS@` and `@OUT@` to fill in.
- `brief-grader.md`: the grader's brief. It names the first run's scratch folder; put yours in its place.
- `grades.md`: the first run's blind grading. X is the new entries and Y the old.
- `grades-pilot.md`: the second run's grading, on the consolidation's pilot: one reader in the pilot's copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the old entries and Y the pilot's; 28 and 29 of 30.
- `grades-final.md`: the third run's grading, on the finished consolidation: one reader in its copy, graded against the first run's old-entries answers. X is the finished record and Y the old entries; 30 and 28 of 30.
- `grades-scenario6.md`: scenario 6 run again on the final record (124.1K), its entry F-201 replaced by the `coordinator` skill's section that now holds it; graded by the coordinator, not blind: 3 of 3, as before.

## How to run it

1. Make two worktrees of `main` at one base, detached: `git worktree add --detach /home/user/record-test-p BASE`, and the same for `/home/user/record-test-q`. Copy p keeps the old entries; copy q gets the new ones.
2. In both copies, delete what would tell a reader about the test or show it the other copy's texts, and commit nothing: `explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`, `HELD.md`, `process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md`, this folder, and their lines in `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`.
3. In copy q, put in the new texts. Replace each entry's line with its new text from Part 3, or from Part 3b where the entry is there too, as POSITIONS 48 and 60 are. Write each one with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py set` in the copy, which keeps the old line in the history file. Then run `record.py check --base HEAD` in the copy.
4. Check the placeholders. `questions.md` names each entry by its line number at `0f54a698b`, which is its number since the record was numbered. On another base, check that each number still names the entry that the scenario means (the titles in Parts 3 and 3b; a merged entry's number is gone), and change the number where it does not. `fill.py` checks only that the number names one entry.
5. Fill the questions, once for each copy, into a file outside both copies: `python3 fill.py /home/user/record-test-p questions.md OUT`.
6. Launch one fresh Opus reader in each copy, with `brief-reader.md`: `@DIR@` is the copy, `@QUESTIONS@` its filled questions, `@OUT@` its answers. The two briefs differ in nothing else. Each reader wrote about 0.4M tokens in the first run.
7. Blind the answers. Copy them to `grade/answers-X.md` and `grade/answers-Y.md` by a choice the grader does not see, and write which is which in a file that the grader is not given (`arms.txt` in the first run).
8. Launch one Fable grader with `brief-grader.md`. It reads `questions.md` unfilled, `key.md` and the two answer files, and checks against `main` any claim beyond the key. It wrote 0.75M tokens in the first run.
9. Unblind with the arms file, and report by "the new entries" and "the old entries", not X and Y.

To re-run one scenario after an entry is repaired, cut `questions.md` to that scenario, fill it from the copy, and give a fresh reader the same brief. Grade it against the same key. In the first run, the coordinator graded the re-run of scenario 7 itself, knowing its copy, so that grade was not blind.

Yes, I used them wrongly. The workflows are in the skill's part on the record, under "The consolidation tools". My plan this morning would have repeated the same mistake. The brief I gave the run is now pushed: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/foundations/evidence/rewrite/run-brief.md

Noted: Fable may edit a batch record. I won't bring a proposal about its edits to 22c's record.

**How I used the clarity workflow wrongly**
1. The workflow exists to make entries clear, and its writer must keep each entry's meaning. It works from your own words, which the mining workflow collected. I used it to change what the entries say.
2. I changed its script so that it took a brief of my own (commit `bedc80b01`). That brief went to the writer, the fix round, the checker and the judge. It said "Where they differ, this brief wins." So my brief replaced the workflow's own rules.
3. My brief made the Fable judgement's list of behaviours "the target". Each new text had to produce every behaviour on that list. The checker and the judge counted a missing behaviour as a failure. So the checks made the texts grow.
4. My brief put the judgement first among the sources and your words second. The workflow puts your words first.
5. My brief told the writer to give the year of each ground. The record's rule says a date goes into the history, not into the entry.
6. My brief asked for more content in the entries:
   - the layer of each ground;
   - the three layers defined in the entry on the team's later word;
   - which grounds were measured and which were not.
7. The run covered 13 entries. You had said yes to rewording two: the entry on one library and the entry on the team's later word. I widened the scope on my own.
8. I didn't run the record's length check before I showed you the texts. Together the 13 texts went from 11.2K to 21.2K characters. That is about 1.6K each, against the record's guide of about 600 characters.

**How I used the test wrongly**
- The test kit asks one thing: does a reader decide as well from the new entries as from the old ones? It can't detect length, register or dates.
- The record's own pass checks length, register and dates, and so does your reading. I let the passed test stand in for both.

**What the right use would be (my reading, not checked yet)**
- **Small corrections:** the skill names the mining workflow's writer for these. Its first rule says that an entry that is yours and correct stays word for word. Only a sentence that is wrong, not yours, or out of date changes. Another of its rules says that a sentence with no source in your words keeps its text and becomes a question for you.
- **The new evidence:** the foundations review's evidence would go into that workflow as input. The workflow keeps its own briefs, with no brief of mine on top.
- **The clarity workflow:** run it only on an entry that no longer reads on its own, with its own briefs.
- **The checks after:** the record's pass with its length check, and then your reading of each change.

I'd have a worker read the mining workflow's briefs before I propose a run, so we know they fit this use. I also propose removing the hook I added to the clarity script. Then a run brief can't override the workflow's rules again.

content.text:
No. Since 10-26, nobody has changed the mining tool, the test kit, the record tool or the skills. My change to the clarity tool was the only damage, and I have reversed it.

**The goal**
- After a compaction, I must make the right call at a choice point. Two examples: the two libraries differ, or two sources of the team disagree.
- I get the reasons for that call only from POSITIONS. So POSITIONS must hold the understanding that we reached on 10-26.
- Its entries must not contradict each other. Each reason must be in the right layer: the language, the team's JVM implementation, or how Fortress meets Java.
- The entries must stay short and in your register.

**The issues**
1. **A contradiction about the compiler's library.**
   - The entry on one library calls the compiler's library a bootstrap to remove.
   - The entry on flat numbers calls it "the team's last record of the Fortress way".
   - The answer from 10-26: a deliberate later design in that library comes into the one library, and a stub or a JVM workaround does not.
2. **A contradiction about the layers.**
   - The entry on the team's later word counts the team's JVM code as the team's word on the language.
   - Your layer rule says that a reason in one layer does not decide a question in another.
   - The export decision (each abstract api member must be declared in the component) depends on exactly this point.
3. **A missing reason.** The entry on one library does not give your reason: we must not port walk's library into the compiler's library, so the checker improves until it accepts the one library.
4. **A missing date rule.** No entry says that we check "later" by date.
5. **Smaller wrong statements in other entries.** For example:
   - the grounds for the bound `Any`;
   - how much work it is for walk to run the checker;
   - your preference of 09-20 for the class loader, which nobody recorded.

The trap test agrees with issues 3 and 4. With the old entries, the readers went wrong at exactly those two points.

**The sources that we can keep**
- **The evidence reports**, all written by Opus or Sonnet:
  - the history of the bound `Object`;
  - the probe of the bound `Any`;
  - the map of evidence for the nine foundational decisions;
  - the sweep of the places where the two libraries differ.
- **The reasoning of the Fable judgement.** It says, entry by entry, what is wrong. We keep its points, not its words.
- **Your words of 10-25 and 10-26**, in the conversation note.
- **The trap test.** Its four scenarios and its answer key already exist, and we can run them again.
- **What we can't keep:** the 13 rewritten texts and their page.

**The tools**
- **Your yes.** Each correction changes the text of one of your decisions, so each one needs your yes on its wording. The review queue holds the items that wait for your word.
- **The trap test kit.** It checks the goal: do the readers make the right call?
- **The record's pass and the record tool's check.** They check the form: the length, no dates, one subject per entry.
- **The mining tool.** It shows whether a reason came from your words or from an agent. We need it where a reason may not be yours, as in the entry on flat numbers.
- **The clarity tool.** It rewrites the wording of an entry and must keep the meaning. We use it only if an entry is still hard to read after a correction.
- **Opus** writes every text. **Fable** may only comment on it.

**What I don't know yet**
- I don't know which tool should write the corrections themselves.
- The mining tool's writer changes as little as possible, which fits this work. But it was built to check where an entry came from, not to apply new evidence.

If this framing is still wrong, please tell me which part.
